I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Tolmie :
That the order for the third reading of Bill (No. 57) to incorporate the Crow's Nest Southern Railway Company be discharged, that the Bill be withdrawn, and that the fees paid thereon be refunded, less the expense of printing the same.
I hope the hon. gentleman will tell us in a few words the reason for the withdrawal of this Bill.
The promoters of the Bill wish to withdraw it.

Why ? They came to this House and asked for a certain charter and there has been a great deal of discussion throughout the country in regard to this measure. Now ithat this Bill is to be withdrawn, a short explanation should come from the hon. gentleman or from some member of the government in regard to it.

In view of what we see in the papers it would be in order to have some explanation. It is said that the promoters have decided to withdraw it because of an understanding with the Dominion government, that they may build to the boundary line under a provincial charter, and there connect with a road In the United States. If they do that, they must do it in violation of the law which compels them to come to the Dominion parliament for power to cross the boundary line by a railway. The Bill as amended in the committee, guaranteed that the people of the North-west and British Columbia could buy the product of the Crow's Nest Pass coal mines at as low a price as it would be sold to people south of the boundary line. It is interesting for the people of Canada, and especially the people of British Columbia to know what has become of that.

When this Bill was before the Railway Committee it was understood that the promoters were to sign a certain agreement. This agreement has not been signed and therefore the government cannot agree to the passage of this Bill. The promoters have consequently withdrawn it. I understand that a charter has been given to the same company by the legislature of British Columbia. The government have not received that charter yet and do not know what the terms of it are, and therefore it is impossible to make a statement as to what is the attitude of the government on that point.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: Has the agreement referred to been made public ?
Yes, it was before the Railway Committee.

That the rules and orders of the House be suspended as regards Bill (No. 19) to amend the Act passed during the present session entitled :
' An Act to incorporate the Fort Qu'Appelle Railway Company,' and that permission be given by the House that this Bill take all its stages forthwith.
I may say that the Bill is only to change a single word and there was no opposition to it in the Senate.
What is the change 7
Simply taking out the word electric ' and putting In ' a railway.'
Well, that is quite a change from an electric railway to a steam railway, and yet the hon. gentleman says it is of no importance.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first and the second time.
Mr. DOUGLAS moved that the House resolve itself into committee on the Bill.

I understand that the Railway Committee is decidedly adverse to this proposed change because there was not sufficient notice of it, or something of that kind. We are certainly violating the rules in this procedure now.
The objection of the hon. gentleman is well taken, but I am informed there has only been a change in one word, which is of no importance.
It may be of great importance.
We will see that when we get into committee.

My recollection is that application was made for a charter for a railway from a junction on the Canadian Pacific Railway to Fort Qu'Appelle. There was no objection to it being either an electric or a steam road, but some of the promoters wanted to make it an electric road, and the hon. member representing the district wishes to give them power to operate a steam road if necessary. The only possible connection at present is with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I cannot imagine any objection to allowing them to have a steam road.

When a Bill is advertised and people read the advertisement, they suppose that a Bill on the lines of that advertisement is to be introduced and passed by the House. In this case the notice refers to an electric railway, and now it is proposed to change it to a steam railway. I think this should not be allowed, because though the promoter of the Bill and others say that there is no opposition to this, we do not know what opposition to it might develop in that part of the country if the people were aware that such a railway was being asked for.

The difficulty is this, that oue portion of the Act applies only to electric railways and the other portion only to steam railways. This passed the committee as an electric railway. Now it is proposed to change it to a steam railway, and the question is, how are you going to make that portion of the Railway Act referring to steam railways apply to it ?
The change seems to be perfectly technical, but of course if there is an objection taken to the Bill it cannot proceed.

The only question seems to be whether or not the notice covered this Bill. Only a few days ago we* sent a Bill back to the. Standing Orders Committee to see whether the notice covered a change in it. If the notice covers this change, I see no possible objection to it but if the notice does not cover it, I do not see how we can act differently in this case from what we did in the other case.

If we had time to look into all these points, we might settle them ; but we have no time, and therefore I think the Bill should be referred back to the Railway Committee.
Motion of Mr. Douglas withdrawn, find Bill referred back to the Railway Committee.

LEAD BOUNTIES. *
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following resolution :
Resolved, That it is expedient to provide as follows in order to encourage the refining of lead in Canada :-
1.	That the Governor in Council may authorize the payment of the undermentioned bounties on lead refined in Canada from materials produced in Canadian smelters from Canadian lead ore-
(a)	On every ton of lead so refined during the calendar year 1902, $5.
(b)	On every ton of lead so refined during the calendar year of 1903, $4.
(c)	On every ton of lead so refined during the calendar year of 1904, $3.

571S
(d)	On every ton of lead so refined during the calendar year of 1905, $2.
(e)	On every ton of lead so refined during the calendar year of 1906, $1.
2.	The said bounties shall he payable halfyearly on the first days of July and January in each year.
3.	The total sum payable for such bounties shall not exceed $100,000 in any year.
If the sum payable at the rates per ton mentioned in resolution (1) on lead refined during the half of any calendar year shall exceed $50,000, then and in such case the bounty payable per ton shall be reduced as regards that halfyear to such rate per ton as shall make the amount of bounties payable in respect of such half-year not more than $50,000.
4.	If the sum paid for such bounties in any half-year shall be less than $50,000, the unpaid balance (being the difference between the sum so paid and $50,000) shall be carried to the credit of the bounty fund for the next succeeding half-year and may be paid out in such succeeding half-year in addition to the $50,000 hereinbefore provided.
5.	The Governor in Council may make such rules and regulations (including regulations as to rates and charges for refining) as may be deemed expedient in the public interest, for carrying out the purposes of this Act, and all payments of bounty shall be subject to the due observance of such rules and regulations.
6.	All bounties payable under these resolutions shall cease and determine on the thirty-first day of December, 1906.
He said : for many years the silver lead mining industry of British Columbia has been recognized as one of very considerable importance. There are three stages to the industry : First, the mining of the ore ; second, the treatment of the ore in the smelter, and third, the final stage of refining the product of the smelter at the refinery, where the various elements which enter into the bullion are separated, and refined lead and silver, etc., are turned out. Some years go we thought it desirable to encourage, not merely the mining of ore but the smelting, and in 1895 an Act was passed encouraging the smelting of the silver lead ores of Canada to the extent of $150,000. That Act has ceased to operate, but under Its operations several smelters were established. There are at present two in existence-one at Trail and one at Nelson. The business had a fair development, and there was every prospect of continued development until a very recent date. Under fair conditions, there would probably have been an output of silver lead ore in Canada this year of 100,000 tons, but, unfortunately, events in the United States have placed the Canadian enterprise at such a great disadvantage that it becomes a question whether the industry can continue at all. The lead companies of the United States have been consolidated into one large concern, known as the American Smelting and Refining Company, with a capital of $60,000,000, and it is reported in the press recently that that company has united its forces
with several of the great copper companies of the United States, and that the united capital of these enterprises will amount to about $500,000,000. Hitherto we have been able to sell in the United States our ores from the mine or our bullion from the smelters, but of late the Americans have taken it into their heads not to deal very liberally with Canada. The American tariff is so regulated as to give every possible encouragement to their own industry, under the operation of which it is very difficult for us to send our products into the United States. Then there is a certain advantage in the American system of refining, which operates in their favour and against us to a certain extent. The Americans refine foreign ores in bond, and are permitted to export 90 per cent of that and treat that 90 per cent as the Whole quantity. Thus, if they import $100,000 worth of lead in the ore and export 90 per cent of that, the 90 per cent exported is considered equivalent to the whole, and the 10 per cent remaining can be sold in the United States, where the lead market is the highest In the world. In that way, as well as by their general tariff policy, the Americans encourage their lead refining Industry. Of late they have declined to purchase our lead ores at all. They still consent to receive the bullion from the smelters and treat it in their refineries, but will only do so at a very large advantage in the cost of treatment, so that by these various means the business is being concen-, trated in the United States, and it becomes a question whether or not we will have any lead industry in Canada at all. We think that the policy now introduced is worthy of a fair trial. The conditions in Canada are favourable, and we ought to be able to establish the industry on a permanent basis. We therefore propose to do now for the refining industry what was done five or six years ago for the smelting industry. At first we had only the mining of the ores, then we granted bounties on the smelting of them, and now we desire to go a step further and say that, within moderate limits and for a reasonable period, we will grant bounties on the refining of lead in Canada, so that we may have within our own borders all the processes of manufacture carried on.
As to the extent to which we should aid this enterprise, that is a matter for consideration. The business involves a very large capital. It is not merely in the erection of a refinery, but the handling of the article that large capital is required. The company which will go into this business must not only establish a refinery, which in itself involves a capital expenditure of '$250,000 or more, but provide large capital to carry on the enterprise. The product has to be carried in stock a very considerable period, and if any company wants to go into the business, it will require a capital of $1,000,000 to $2,000,000. We have come to the con-

elusion to offer bounties on a sliding scale. The applicants aslced for a much more liberal bounty than we are granting, but no doubt that is the case in all such applications for government assistance. We hope, however, that with the aid of bounties on the scale we have laid down in this resolution, the industry will be established.
We propose beginning with the 1st January next-because we assume that some months will pass before a refinery can be established-to allow to any party wno established a lead refinery in Canada a bounty of $5 a ton for the first year, limited, however, to $100,000 per annum. For the second year we propose that the bounty shall be $4 per ton ; the third year, $3 per ton ; the fourth year, $2 per ton ; and finally, $1 per ton. We think that this system of bounties, if it is to be established, should be based upon the principle of gradually wiping the bounty out. Wherever you give a bounty to an industry of an even sum continually, tlie tendency is for the industry to rely bin the bounty to such an extent that the sudden cutting off of the bounty at the end of the term would so change the condition as, perhaps, to put the industry in peril. We think it best, therefore, while giving the aid that the government are disposed to give, to let the industry understand that it must look forward at a very early date to standing upon its own bottom, Therefore, we follow the system of reducing [DOT]the bounties year by year until at the end of the fifth year they cease and determine. And we propose to limit the total amount to $100,000 per annum. We anticipate that this will be no undue restriction upon the industry, but, perhaps in granting the bounties, we shall all feel better if we have a clear conception of the amount to which we ax-e obliged. In the case of iron and steel, there is no limit to the quantity upon which a bounty shall be paid, and so we may be called upon to pay a larger sum than we originally anticipated. In this case, we think it well that the House and the country should understand the extent to which the obligation is to go. Therefore, for the first year it will cost $100,000 on the basis of $5 a ton ; and if as the bounty per ton falls year by year their output increases, they may still get the benefit of tlie $100,000 at tlie lower rates. Then, we propose to make it cumulative as respects one year. That is if through any mishap the output in the first half of the year should be too small to earn half of the total maximum bounty, and, in the next six months the output should so increase as to earn more than half the maximum bounty, we propose that they shall still have the benefit of the total amount of $100,000 in one year.
What about the next year ?
Each year will be complete within itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: The output of one year would not be available to earn part of another year's bounty ?

No, each year must be within Itself, and not more than $100,000 will be paid In any one year. It might happen that, owing to the suspension of the work or to some other cause they might, in six months not turn out enough to earn $50,000. In that case, we would credit them with the balance on the next six months, so that if they earned the $100,000 within the year that amount would be paid them.
But, in case there should be an excess in the year, that would not be available for bounty for the first six months of the year ?

No, it does not pass from one year to another, but it does pass from tlie first six months to tlie second six months of one year. We make it half-yearly so as to suit a reasonable business convenience. But with each year the transaction closes and we start upon a fresh year.
That is, there may be more than $50,000 in one half year, but there cannot be more than $100,000 in any one year.
My bon. friend is quite correct.

Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Finance to give the House information as to the value to the United States refineries of the protection which he has referred to namely, the permission given them to export 90 per cent of what has been refined instead of tlie entire amount. We ought to know what that is worth to the American refiners in order to judge of the adequacy of the bounty proposed. Another point on which I would like information is the extent of tlie industry in Canada.

I shall have my papers here in a moment, but I am without them just now, because this question has come forward sooner than 1 expected. But I believe that the output of the product of the silver-lead ores of Canada from 1888 to 1900 represented a total value of about $20,000,000. During 1900 tlie value of these ores represented a total value of $5,000,000. There would be every prospect of the output increasing if we had the facilities for production. As to the value of this 10 per cent concession in the United States, it is represented to me that it is equivalent to $5 a ton. That figure I can only give from information supplied me by gentlemen interested in the lead industry. While necessarily this industry will have to be established by some one or two large companies-

not more than one I believe-the government bad before them a large deputation representing all interests in the lead business in British Columbia, these gentlejnen attaching so much importance to the matter tlial they came all the way from British Colum bia to Ottawa to present their case to the government, and I have reason to believe that the miners, the smelters and all eon cerned join in approving this scheme. For though the bounty will go to the refinery, it is realized that without a refinery you cannot have a smelter, and without a smelter you cannot have business for the miner.

The significant fact about this is that at last the government confess before the country that it is possible for the government to bring in such legislation as will develop the interests of the country and will protect the industries of the country against the unfair attacks of other nations. For a long time the Liberal party denied the principle of protection and that of paternal government. But now wo see them confessing that they believe in customs duties, not only ad valorem, but specific duties ; confessing that they believe in export duties-they are insisting on our logs being manufactured in Canada-we find them confessing that they believe in bounties of all kinds. Here is a bounty which proves it. And, still more significant than their proposal, is the fact that the knight from Oxford (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) with an eloquence unequalled in the history of this country, approves these things that for twenty-five years he condemned. His silent eloquence is the greatest endorsement that protectionist jjrinciples have ever received in this country. I take this opportunity now of at last congratulating the Liberal party on this forward step, and of congratulating the hon. member for South Oxford upon the eloquent silence with which he gives it his approval. What follows from the platform thus laid down by the Liberal party ? They must go one step further and adopt the principle of reciprocity of tariffs. To-day Canada is suffering from the hostile tariff of the United States which is designed to keep Canadian manufacturers out of the American market and out of the -markets of the world, if that can be done. We want but one thing more in the line of national policy, and we are coming to it. The Liberal party will be forced to adopt it, and the hon. member for South Oxford will be compelled to give it his eloquently silent support, and that is the principle of tariff for tariff as the only way in which Canada can hold her own in the face of the competition of the United States.

I do not wish to follow' the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) in his reflections on general principles, for I think that the country know's very well now that wre have protection. But, as a moderate
protectionist, I begin to fear that the government is going a little too far in the way of protection.
There was an industry which attracted a good deal of capital to this country, the phosphate industry, which existed mainly in the province of Quebec. I do not know if some of the members of this House have known of the details of this industry, but I may say that at one time it was one of the most prosperous mining industries of this country. It was carried on specially in the northern regions of the Ottawa valley, w'here several mines were in operation. Large amounts of British, American and French capital were invested in this industry. But competition arose from the discovery of an inferior quality of phosphate in Algeria, Florida and the Argentine Republic.
Although the phosphate of the Lievre valley was no doubt the best phosphate in the world, so aeknow'ledged in the exhibition of Philadelphia and in the French exhibition in 1878, at the same time the cost of working the mines being heavier than the the cost of mining in Florida and the Argentine Republic, the result was that all our Canadian mines have been closed. Several times, the owners of these mines have agitated the question of getting a bounty from a Canadian government. I think, even this winter proceedings were taken by some of the owners of those mines to get a bounty from the government. I was asked by some of those gentlemen, or the representatives of some of those companies, to urge their request before this parliament. I told them frankly that I thought the government and the majority in parliament were not in favour of bounties ; that they had been elected upon a free-trade platform to some extent; and they had kept the bounty on iron only because, as the Minister of BMnance said at the time, the iron-smelting industry had been developed by the establishment of these bounties, and it would not be wise to abolish them. 1 agreed at that time with the Minister of Finance, as X agree with him in regard to this present resolution ; but at the same time, if bounties are to be given to new industries, to interests that will be localized in a smaller territory than the phosphate industry, I do not see why an industry that had prospered in this country for many years and had attracted some $30,000,000, and gave work to several thousands of Canadian miners, should be refused, when they ask a smaller bounty than that which is given to any other Canadian industry. I understand, the owners of the phosphate mines would be satisfied with a bounty of $2 a year upon every ton of the article they manufacture and export. They do not ask for a bounty upon the article they sell in Canada. The development of this industry would mean not only employment for Canadian workingmen"; but it would mean a great assistance to Canadian farmers, because it would develop one of the best fertilizers

known in modern agriculture. In fact, phosphate of lime is one of the fertilizers that have enabled the Belgian and French farmers to develop their industry as they have been doing for the last few years. Now, chemical fertilizers are one of the most costly articles which the Canadian farmer has to use for the improvement of his farm ; but here is an industry the raw material of which is in the very heart of Canada, on the border of the Ottawa river, with good navigation and railway communication, an industry which could command an immense amount of capital, involving chiefly hand labour, an industry which has been taken up and abandoned because it had no encouragement and because the competition of foreign phosphates was too great for it to overcome. I do not want to make any objection to this bounty on lead, but I hope the government will remember the claim of the phosphate industry, which is so essentially a Canadian industry, and that next year they will be prepared to give it a bounty.

I agreed with the establishment of the bounty on iron, and I do not object to this proposal to give a bounty on lead, because it is fallowing the lines of protection, which I am in favour of. If we can start any industry in this country by means of bounties, I think it is proper to do so. "With reference to the production of phosphates, I was in favour of it years ago, and am still. I was in favour of it for the double reason that it would be the means of starting the industry, and because it would furnish an article very useful to the farmers, as the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bou-rassa) says. But I regretted to find that while this government were prepared to assist the development of the iron industry, an industry which does not benefit the farmers at all directly, when a proposal was made to put a bounty upon beet-root sugar, that directly affected the farmers advantageously, and upon the production of phosphates, which would be of great use to the farmers, the government turned a deaf ear to appeals in their behalf. I regretted that, because it would be simply following the principle of protection in another form which we have always advocated. The action of the government to-day is a compliment to the principles the Conservative party have advocated for so long a time. It is an action taken on the extreme lines of protection for the purpose of bringing into existence industries that could not otherwise be started. But while the present action of the government is a compliment to the soundness of the principles supported by their predecessors, it is another nail in their coffin with regard to the policy they have always advocated in the past.

I will not dis-*cuss the theoretical question of whether this Mr. BOURASSA.
is in line with protection or not. I am quite satisfied modestly to accept the compliments of the hon. gentleman, whether they are deserved or not; providing we get to the end of the session, we can well afford to forego a discussion as to whether we are on the right path. The only point that seems to be apparent is that everybody wants a bounty for himself. Even my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), who is a moderate protectionist, thought we were going too far, if I followed his argument rightly, because we go to British Columbia to give bounty to the lead industry ; but if we only went to the county of Labelle, we would go far enough to satisfy him.
Not only the county of Labelle, but the county of Wright and the whole province of Quebec.

The province of Quebec does not fare badly, I think. But the question is, whether we should give a bounty on phosphates. My hon. friend does not object to a bounty on -lead, but he wants it extended to phosphates. I will not at this moment express an opinion whether we should give a bounty on phosphates. But I will observe that the conditions are not at all parallel. We are forced to give this bounty on lead simply because the Belgian government, in their tariff, have taken a most unfair advantage of our smelters and our lead deposits. Under a natural condition of things there would be no necessity for a bounty. If we had reciprocity in minerals, with the United States there would be no necessity whatever for a bounty in Canada, we would have an ample field in the United States. I think with reciprocity in minerals we could undersell the Americans and take their market from them.
Do you think they will ever allow you to do that ?

That is a question for the future, I do not know, I make no prophecy. But if we are to get it, I doubt if we will get it by the methods proposed by my hon. friend. Moreover, if we were to give bounties and meet the Americans with their tariff, I am not prepared to say that we should go as far as my hon. friend would have us go. But, to come back to the question of the phosphate industry, my hon. friend from Labelle has stated that it was a prosperous industry a few years ago, and so it was. But all of a sudden, without any hostile legislation in any part of the world, it dropped, and why ? The hon. gentleman stated truly a moment ago, that our phosphate industry was- destroyed by the discovery of phosphates in Florida. But the conditions are not parallel. The phosphates in Algeria, in Florida, and, I think, in the Argentine Republic, are called, I think, vegetable phosphates. They have only to dig, they have to open a seam, and there

they have it without any cost of production, whereas, our prospects are different, as the mineral has to be reduced, and, therefore, the produciton of it must cost much more than the production of phosphates in Florida.
Under such circumstances I must say to my hon. friend that I have been approached [DOT]upon more than one occasion personally by people with the view of securing the granting of a bounty on phosphates, hut I have not had up to this day any satisfactory calculation laid before me as to the difference of the cost of production in Florida, our chief competitor, and the cost of production in Canada. While some of the owners of phosphate minerals in the Laurentian range in the province of Quebec have approached me personally in regard to having a bounty of $2 a ton placed upon the production of these minerals, up to this moment I have never seen the calculation upon which that bounty is based, showing the relative cost in Florida and in Canada. We can easily estimate what the cost of production in Canada would be, but if we are to be asked to give a bounty upon that industry my hon. friend would be the first to admit that we cannot entertain a proposition of that kind unless all the calculations are placed before us which would justify us in giving a bounty of $2, or $3 or $1 a ton, and so it is that we have not been able up to this time to ascertain on what this proposed bounty is based. When the application is made we shall have to look at it as we have to look at every application of a similar character which is made to us.

Mr. Chairman, I would just like to emphasize the difference between the conditions in regard to the phosphate industry and in regard to the lead industry in the matter of bonuses. The difference is *that the claim for a bonus for lead refining is not based upon the possibility of competition from other countries overthrowing our market. It is based upon the special conditions existing in the United States, not so much because of the tariff, as because of the combine which exists under that tariff. The proposal to bonus the lead refining industry is a means taken by this country as a whole to meet the combine of lead refiners and smelters of the United States. This is adopted as an experiment or as a temporary expedient for the purpose of putting our industry in a position, not whereby it can compete, but whereby it can be carried on as it cannot be carried on independent of the conditions imposed by the combine in the United States. It is not the case that the lead and silver mines of Canada do not produce sufficiently profitably to enable them to be carried on. They do produce profitably, as profitably as any other mines in the world, so profitably that if the process of putting refined lead on the market can be carried through that process can be maintained without government bonus or assistance. This is the argument that has been
placed before the government, and this is the argument that is being placed before the House. It is not that we have an industry in British Columbia that is not able to stand upon its feet other conditions being equal. Has the hon. gentleman any complete plan for carrying out the work in Toronto harbour ? With the amounts proposed here, no practical result can be accomplished in the way of permanently improving the harbour.

The question of the diversion of thg Don has been before my predecessors for a good many years and before myself ever since I came into office. I have sent for a plan, which will be here is a few moments, and which will explain the whole matter. The harbour of Toronto is being filled up by the silt brought down by the Don and also by the sewarage of the city, and for neither of these is the government responsible. The Don, which was naturally a crooked stream, was straightened by the city years ago. The result of that straightening has been that the silt and material of all kinds came down the Don in such large quantities as to fill the Toronto harbour. But the Toronto harbour is also filled up by the sewage. There are fourteen miles of sewage flowing into Toronto harbour. I do not propose to spend one dollar of public money in the port of Toronto, I will not budge until the city takes care of their own sewage. I cannot be expected to do anything else. I feel that we are not responsible for filling the harbour through the Don. Toronto is an important harbour, but it has no revenue, and the government has taken care of it. I feel we are doing only what is right in asking parliament to vote that sum of money. I

have here a plan which I offer to the inspection of members who take an interest in the harbour of Toronto. Under these circumstances I think I am justified in asking for $25,000. It will not be enough, our proposed work will cost more. But the city must first arrange with me. As soon as I have an arrangement with the city I am prepared to go on.

The city of Toronto has taken care of the sewage which falls into the bay, week by week and month by month. They are taking care of the sewage at their own expense, and I am sorry the Minister of Public Works has adopted this excuse in order to relieve him from the duty of making a fair appropriation to enable vessels of the capacity of the St. Lawrence canal to come into Toronto harbour. If the city of Toronto diverted the Don years ago, they did it with the approval of the government, and the government are legally liable to right the matter. We see large sums of money being expended by this government all over the country, in Halifax, St. John,-a bridge at Quebec, advancing $1,500,000 on certain bonds to help the city of Quebec ; we see appropriations made in places where we have been told this morning there is no revenue. We see the city of Montreal coming here and asking for a million dollars for an elevator, and getting it without any excuse from the government. But here is the greatest shipping centre in this country, a city which gathers more freight and sends out more freight than any other city in this country ; we see the Minister of Public Works endeavouring to find an excuse by which he can evade the liability which falls upon the government of improving Toronto harbour and putting it in such a shape that the vessels which pass up and down Lake Ontario and through the canals may get into that harbour, in order that it may receive vessels that are going to do business between the maritime provinces and the upper lakes, cultivating an interprovincial trade with the maritime provinces in water bound traffic. We cannot participate in this traffic, because the harbour is filled up with silt which has been brought down from the back country year after year. I say that is not fair treatment of the city of Toronto, considering the amount of business that is being done there. But the hon. minister says that before anything is done the city must come here and bind itself to take care of its sewage, which, however, furnishes very little deposit indeed as compared with the amount of silt. In any case I am prepared to say that the city is taking care of its sewage, they are dredging it out of the harbour as fast as it comes in. I hope the minister will reconsider this vote, and make an appropriation which will meet the need, and put the city in a position to accommodate vessels of the capacity of the St. Lawrence canal, vessels

that visit other lake ports and the maritime provinces. I notice on the following page $8,000 for dredging the channel at the mouth of the River Thames. Now if it would faci-liate the improvement of Toronto harbour, I would be very glad to resign my seat in this House, but I am afraid it would not be of any avail, because I am not a supporter of the government. I do not think that is a fair way to treat the people of this country. It is essential for the mercantile interests, not only of the city of Toronto, but of the whole province of Ontario, that that harbour shall have the necessary expenditure upon it, so that it may have its share of the great work of transportation which will go on from year to year in the inland waters of the Dominion. I hope the minister will give us a specific and definite statement as to his intention respecting the plan of that harbour work.

Toronto is very near Ottawa; only a few hours away. The city of Toronto is approachable to other members as I am an approachable man myself, and I am going to approach the municipal authorities of Toronto. I am going to have an understanding with them, and before I have that understanding I will not budge. Without a very clear statement I will not do anything. My hon. friend must not ask me to go quicker than I am in the habit of going. I think I am suggesting a very fair proposition to the city of Toronto. Let them remove these sewers. The work that is described in these estimates does not call for the expenditure of an amount of very great magnitude.
All the more reason why the work should go on.

These estimates will carry out the work because it is not a large work at all. I am going to go to Toronto as soon as the session is over, a week or two afterwards. The

city council would be glad to see me I am sure.	.

Hear, hear.
Mi-. MACLEAN. They would use you well.
I will discuss matters and arrange with them.
Will the hou. Minister of Public Works tell us any case in which he lias refused to budge until the local authorities have come to an agreement with him in a similar matter ?
This is a special case. There are not many cities or localities where there are fourteen sewers unloading the dirt of the city into the harbour.

Toronto is an important harbour as the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) says. It is a harbour upon which if a very little money is spent will show substantial results. We are voting large sums of money for docks and wharfs that will give no results to the country at all. I hope the hon. minister will come up to Toronto. He will find the city disposed to meet him in removing the trouble caused by the sewerage system. I believe the sewerage system is responsible in a measure for it, and I think the city of Toronto would only consult the public health if they deal with that problem. The minister must go to Toronto prepared to do something for Toronto, and I think he may rest assured that he will be well received and that he will find the city of Toronto ready to meet him.
I want to know, when I have placed this amount in the estimates if I do not mean to do something ?
What day shall we set for you to he there ?
The first day my hon. friend is able to stand a first-class lunch, I will go up there.
All right we shall have it.

Strike it out.

Mr. Chairman, before this item passes, I want to refer to a statement made by the hon. Minister of Public Works before the committee rose. He suggested that the hon. member for Toronto did not, perhaps, properly appreciate the difficulties he had to contend with in getting this item into the estimates at all. I think the hon. members from Toronto will appreciate that fact, as many hon. members on this side of the House do appreciate, it very highly. The difficulty which the hon. minister has to keep his colleagues in order, to get proper amounts placed in the estimates in certain cases, and to control the amounts in certain other cases is very great, I have no doubt, and when he does come to the rescue, as he has done in this case, his action should be appreciated on this side of the House. But, in reference to making Toronto harbour what it should be, I wish to say, and I think the committee will agree with me that whenever it is ascertained that there is a necessity for a public work to be executed in the public interests in any part of the country it is desirable that a sufficient amount should be put in the estimates to complete it. Until this is done the money that will have been expended this year, for instance, perhaps, will have very little effect. It seems to me to be beyond argument that the harbour of Toronto should be made available for the vessels which are able to navigate the St. Law-repce canals, and that the time has come to put a sufiicient amount in the estimates to make that harbour available in order to give us direct results from the money expended. Now, in every effort the hon. minister makes, notwithstanding difficulties he encounters on the part of other members of the cabinet, he will, I am sure, have the general support of this side of the House. It is not a question of how much money has been spent in Toronto in the past. That is rather an argument, I apprehend, for voting an amount additional to what has been expended, in order to make that money available and remunerative. So I hope that the hon. minister, if he does not see his way to completing that work this year, will put a larger amount in the estimates next year.

I have already seen my way, for I am carrying out just the work to which the hon. gentleman alludes. We are dredging the entrance to a depth of 16 feet at this very hour. The money I am taking isi for the work to which the hon. gentleman alludes.
Does the minister think this $25,000 will divert the Don ?
No.

Let my hon. friend remember that for nearly every work of importance we vote a certain sum of money each year.
Oakville-Repairs to east pier, &c., $6,000.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if it is his intention to spend this money this summer ?
Yes, and complete the work.
Will it be by tender or by day's work ?

It is necessary to do it by day's labour, as it is a work of repairs. My hon. friend knows that as well as I do.
Blind River-Wharf, $2,500.
May I ask the minister where this place is, and whether it is the construction of a new dock or the purchase of a dock from some person ?
It is the construction of a new dock in the north channel of the Georgian Bay. It is a pretty important place and is developing rapidly.
Is there any private dock there now 7 If not, is that due to the fact that no person has considered it worth investing money in one ?

No, it is no evidence of that at all. This government has built hundreds of wharfs throughout the country ; and the fact that we have built them is no evidence that they are not necessary. Take a small community of 500 people, farmers or fishermen, who want to have a steamer or schooner call at their place. They cannot build a wharf for themselves. If my hon. friend during the recess, when he has some leisure, will look at the public accounts of the past, he will find that most of the wharfs, in Ontario especially, which have been built by private money have not been kept up, and the government has been obliged to take over these works and repair them. We must take things as they are in this world, not as we would like to have them.

I have no remarks to make in regard to places in other provinces where the government have built docks ; but in the province of Ontario it has not been usual for the government to build these docks. In the city of Toronto there is not a government dock. People go there and buy the water front from the government or

from private parties, and erect docks as investments. While the minister has never made any protestations of economy on this score, old members of the House will remember that when the Liberals were on this side of the House they denounced in season and out of season expenditures just similar to this. Now, what is to be done ? The minister has laid it down as a rule that wherever political leverage is applied-because that must have been the case in this instance-and wherever the member for the district supporting the government can make it appear that the parties living in the neighbourhood are not prepared to build a dock, the government will build it for them. There must come an end to this thing some time or other. I do not blame the minister personally ; I think if hej allowed his own judgment to sway him, he would not do this ; but it is done in response to appeals from his party friends. Take the case of Toronto. Here is a harbour which, if it were made deep enough for vessels of large draft, would be a benefit to the whole province ; and yet while the minister is spending thousands of dollars on docks throughout the country from which there will not be a single cent of revenue derivable, and many of which are being actually built alongside of the docks of private parties and rendering them useless, he is neglecting the harbour of Toronto. The country will understand some day that the minister is amenable to the influence and suggestions of his party friends.

Hon. gentlemen must understand that the trade of this country is developing. There are farming communities and industrial communities rising from the ground, so to speak, every day. Our waterways are most important to the farming and other industries of the country, and a small wharf for a small community of 400 or 500 people is just as important to them as the big docks we are now erecting iu Montreal ; and I think that every Minister of Public Works who knows his duty will do just what I am doing. When a small fishing or farming community presents a petition to me representing that they cannot sell their products without a small wharf, I give them the wharf whenever my colleagues allow me.
May 1 ask the minister if the erection of these docks is due to the fact that there is commerce to come from them 7

Certainly. The farmers are the greatest traders in this country. Theyi have rights, and one of the best accommodations they can have are these small wharfs. They do not cost much money. Two or three thousand dollars to equip a small farming community is in my opinion well invested money.
If the minister wants to go along that line, that the greater amount of traffic that is to be concentrated at a point, the more necessity for the dock, then the larger points should have docks also.
Certainly. I do not neglect the big points.

Then, why does the hou. minister not go right to the city of Toronto, where, if there were deep enough water, there would be hundreds of boats where there is but one calling at small points like Blind River ?
Is there not a wharf at Toronto ?
Are we not doing the right thing by Toronto ?

There are scores of wharfs at Toronto, but ail built by private parties. Those parties purchased the water lots and built the docks. Any steamboat companies that wish to call at these docks must pay toll, and our contention is that, these steamboat people are using these docks which we have constructed all along the shores, free of rent, while the country pays the piper.
No.
The hon. minister says no. Let me instance the wharf at a pornt called Thessalon. The Minister of Marine says that not a single dollar of revenue is derived from it.
That dock was built fifteen or twenty years ago. I was not the guilty man. I am only repairing It.

All the more reason why the hon. minister should be guided by the errors of the past. When he sees a government dock there, on which he has to spend money for repairs, and from which he does not get a cent of revenue, why does he go on building similar docks all along the shores of Algoma. When on this side of the House, hon. gentlemen opposite denounced such expenditures by the hour, but this afternoon they swallow them without a word of protest. It is an outrage on the public to be spending the public money solely for the accommodation of steamboat companies. Right at Bruce Mines, there was a private dock for the use of which steamboat companies had to pay rent to the proprietor. But that dock has been made useless by the government building one and not gettiug any revenue. At Murray Bay, the government are spending a large sum for extension of the wharf, and yet the Richelieu Navigation Company did not pay a single dollar last year rental for the use of that
wharf. This kind of thing is going on all over the Dominion.
Let me remind my hon. friend that I never made many speeches of the character he has just described.
I do not blame the hon. gentleman.

During the last twenty-five years I have followed the debates of this House-have missed only two sessions-and I cannot forget that I have always heard the opposition criticise what the government does. When my hon. friends on this side were In opposition, they were just as critical as my hon. friend from Simeoe is now. But circumstances alter cases. However, I happen in this matter to be consistent, because I always approved of expenditure on public works when in opposition and am carrying out my views now, which are cheerfully shared by my hon friends on this side.

Since the hon. minister declares ihimself in favour of building wharfs for the benefit of the farmers at different points, I would draw his attention to a petition from the people at Gordon's Point, for a wharf down there. There is a coast line from Summerside to Charlottetown of over forty miles, and in all that distance there is only one harbour, Crapaud. Cape Traverse wharf, which was built some years ago, has been allowed to get out of repair and is falling into the sea. I believe that some fifty or sixty horses and men were put to work there two or three days before the election and kept on until the day after the election. When my hon. friend, Mr. John Bell, was not returned, the carts were immediately taken off. If this Cape Traverse wharf is not taken hold of at once, the thousands of dollars spent on it will be wasted.

I am glad my hon. frend does not share the views of the hon. member for Simeoe but is quite prepared to allow me to build wharfs in his riding. But I cannot build wharfs every where at once. If, however, he is right in his claim, no doubt the day will come when his wishes will be gratified.

This is simply another evidence of the waste of public money on small docks instead of concentrating the expenditure on .some important public work. The hon. minister delivered a little stump speech a few moments ago with regard to the farmers and small producers in this country. But If he is taking a deep interest in the transportation of agricultural products, he must know that the largest taxpayer of this country is the farmer. The farmer it is who contributes the most of this tremend-

ous expenditure. After the farmer has paid for these wharfs and harbours and subsidies to railways and bridges, every hundred pounds of grain grown in Canada going out to Liverpool or any other port of Europe cost from 2 to 8 cents more than grain transported over the same Canadian route <but grown in the United States. If the hon. gentleman wants to do something for the farmers, he will remove that handicap, and In that way confer a greater benefit on the agricultural community than by building little wharfs here and there. I care not in what province.
I quite share the views expressed by my hon. friend. We are putting forth our best endeavour to have cheap rates.
What are you doing ?

Let my lion. * friend look at the estimates, and he will find that we are doing a great deal. We are dredging the St. Lawrence, widening and deepening the channel; we are equipping the port of Montreal, and Port Colborne and Parry Sound. The hon. gentleman follows public affairs and should not ask what we are doing. We cannot do everything at once. The Minister of Marine has asked for a large amount in order to provide better buoys in Sydney. Perhaps we are not doing everything that could be done, but we have to be careful although we are enjoying a buoyant revenue. On reflection, I think my hon. frend will admit that we are doing a good deal.
I recognize what the hon. gentleman says and he knows full well that I am not at all opposing the expenditures, even though they be large.
I know.

But after we have made those expenditures, our people should realize as much benefit from them as do foreigners. I am here to state that if the hon. gentleman chooses to investigate, he will find that American grain loaded at Midland or any other port, brought to Port 'Colborne or any other port, and transported from Canada via Montreal, Quebec in the summer or from the United States via Boston or Portland in the winter, pays 7 cents less per 100 pounds than does Canadian grain.
That is the point I object to. If you deepen Port Colborne or deepen the channel of the St. Lawrence till doomsday, unless you regulate the freight rates, you will never do justice to the small producer in Canada. For, remember, this grain from the United States goes over precisely the same route, and is even shipped from Montreal under similar conditions. It is carried at these low rates by railway companies Mr. POPE.
and other organizations that have been subsidized with the public money of Canada. This is a handicap, an embargo upon the farmers of this country. And it is not right for this government or any other government to appeal to the farmers, saying : Give us money, because it is for you we are doing all this, for you the small producer. Why, the small producer is paying twice, first for the channel and the improvements that the hon. gentleman wishes to make, and then for the extraordinary freights he has to pay on every car-load that is exported from the country.
And the Yankee pays nothing.

The Yankee pays nothing ? You bet he jrnys nothing. But, he gets the benefits. In fact, this is an inducement to them to grow grain in the United States. It is time the ministry and the House took hold of this question. There is no doubt about the figures I have given, for I have them from the best authority. But, I have no right to any information that the ministry does not possess. If these are the facts, the matter is worthy of attention. We have heard of a railway commission to investigate matters. I was in hopes that something might be done. But, I find, as we are getting to the tail end of this session, that we have to congratulate ourselves on accomplishing only one thing, and that is, increasing our salaries.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Pope) perhaps might have advised our predecessors on this very important question. I would like to ask him if he is in a position to offer an opinion as to the means to be taken to remedy the state of affairs to which he has just alluded. It may be that the Grand Trunk Railway are discriminating in favour of grain carried by Portland. That is a question to which we must give consideration. But, the government is not responsible for that state of affairs. We are taking the means to bring back the Grand Trunk Railway to the port of Montreal by equipping that port as it should be equipped, by deepening and widening the St. Lawrence route, and by making it safe. We cannot do more than that now. As to the transportation commission-I would not speak of a railway commission-speaking, not as a menfber of the government, I take this opportunity of saying, that on many occasions, many and many and many occasions. I find myself incompetent to deal with the important problems that are brought before me. I give them as much attention as I can. Those of my hon. friends on the other side that have been ministers know that our days, and a part of our nights, are taken up with questions of detail which forbid us applying our best attention to which men of the highest ability should give their attention.

Nobody would be more highly pleased than I if the government of the country, be it Liberal or Conservative, were in a position to receive advice from men who would have no political purposes to serve, but who would have only the interests of the country in view. I have been a minister for five years. And I have learned a good deal in that time. But, I have learned that a minister, however well he may mean, whatever his intentions may be, is obliged to consider political exigencies. The affairs of this country are conducted on party lines, but, over and above party lines, there are problems of transportation that a commission could help up to solve, and to solve in a way to advance the best interests of Canada.
As this question has drifted somewhat from the point that you have brought before the committee, Mr. Chairman, perhaps I may be permitted, seeing that the hon. minister has asked for advice
I think I must rule this debate out of order, if it is going to drift to a general consideration of the transportation question.
I have no objection to going on.

The minister has asked for advice. Coming, as I do, from a portion of the Dominion where, possibly, we are more interested in that question than are the people in any other part of the country, I may say that, in my opinion, there is one point that has been lost sight of in this House to a great extent
I think I must call my hon. friend to order. The question before the House is, that of the repairs to this wharf.
But, I was only answering the minister, who said he wanted advice.

My hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) will have an opportunity later on.
Wendover-Wharf, $6,500.
Where is Wendover ?
It is in the riding of Prescott, on the Ottawa river.
What is the purpose of this dock ?
Just the same as I have stated in the other cases. This is to give accommodation to a large population.
Fishermen, this time, or farmers ?
A large farming population.

I am sorry that the remarks from this side seem to have lost their effect. When this question was up before, we had a convert on the other side, an able assistant in protesting against these expenditures, in the person of the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton). I am afraid he is lost to us. There seems to have been much in the argument that this is for the farmer and the fishermen, for he is one of the following of the government applauding this building of docks in unknown and unfrequented places.
Presqu'ile-Purchase of wharf and repair, $5,000.
Where is this wharf ?
This work has been applied for by both political parties. I have a petition signed by hundreds of Liberals and Conservatives, including the president of the Liberal-Conservative association.
I did not ask that. I simply asked where this wharf is.

I am always anxious to give information, but I cannot give it all at one stroke. This is situated at Owen Sound Bay, in a very fine location. The appropriation has been applied for by hundreds of Liberals and Conservatives. I have here the petition which I am prepared to lay on the Table of the House.
As $5,000 is being asked for the purchase of the dock, I would ask who is the vendor, and who has appraised the dock as worth $5,000 ?
The name I have in my notes as the vendor is John Mackenzie. The property has not been bought yet.
But it is to be bought ?
It has to be bought. I am just asking parliament permission to buy this property, following the example that has been set for me by my predecessors on many occasions.
How much for the purchase, and how much for repairs ?
I have not made a bargain yet. I will try to buy as cheaply as I can, but I will not bind myself to any price.

I may be able to throw a little light on this matter. In 1899 the township councils of Keppel and Sarawak, which adjoin this dock, petitioned the gov-

eminent to take it over, for the reason that the present proprietors of the dock were not in a position financially to do such repairs as were necessary if the dock were to be of any further use to the community. Following* up the petition of the two councils, a personal petition was passed round the neighbourhoods which this dock serves, and was signed by everybody in that community. It was signed, I think, by every prominent citizen of Owen Sound, including the present local member for the constituency, and including my political opponent at the last election, as well as myself So that so far as the proposition at present before the committee is concerned, there is no political aspect in it whatever, I think. The purpose which the dock serves is simply this :	It is situated some nine and
a half miles north of the town of Owen Sound, on the western side of Owen Sound harbour. If there were no dock there it would be necessary for the farming communities of those townships to bring their produce, such as their grain, fruit, pressed hay, as well as their cattle, into Owen Sound, necessitating a drive in the case of the cattle of some nine or ten miles. I am not here to say there is much traffic over this dock ; for the past few years there has been practically no traffic whatever, for the reason that the dock itself has not been in such a condition as to allow traffic being carried on over it. Seeing that the dock was going into disrepair, and the present owners of the dock were unable to make the necessary repairs, the question arose whether it was better that the government should take over that dock, or should appropriate a certain amount of money for the repair of a private dock. So far as I am concerned, I am quite prepared to take the stand that it is better the government should take over the dock. I may say that the dock was built in 1863 by the present owner, that it was held as a private dock from that day to this, that no fees or charges whatever from that day to the present time have been made on the people of the community for the use of that dock. As I say, the purchase of that dock is approved by the whole community.
How much is he asking for the dock now ?

He is asking $4,000. There have been statements sent in as to the condition of the dock by men who understand that. The portion that is above water, as well as the storehouses, have gone out of repair. But $1,000, I believe, will put the dock in first-class condition.

From the facts stated by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Horsey) it would seem that some parties away back in the sixties constructed a dock, and no doubt they constructed it as Mr. HORSEY.
an investment, and from that time up to the present, the hon. gentleman says, they have not been able to make any money out of it.
They never charged anything, I said. I did not say they never made any money out of it.

Every man knows that, go where you will, wherever you find private docks, in Toronto, or Midland, or anywhere else, a private party owns the dock, and those who wish to use that dock, carrying produce over it in wagons, are forced, as they should be, to pay a fair remuneration to the owner. Now, what is the case here ? Here is a gentleman, Mr. Mackenzie, not able to make anything out of his dock, and he is unloading it on the government for the price of $4,000. Why, it is easy to understand that the townships won't buy the dock because it is not a good investment, and I will be bound to say that had the townships bought the dock, they would have come in for the strongest censure from the people. The people see that public money is given by thousands for docks from one end of the country to the other, and It is the easiest possible thing to get up a requisition signed by everybody asking the government to pay for this dock. No wonder Mr. Mackenzie could get the signatures he obtained. I have no doubt he pointed to that famous case at Hilton where a party sold a dock for $5,000 to this department that did not cost him $500. That is a notorious fact all through the district of Algoma. And here we have this largely signed petition. I notice one thing about the signatures, that they are all alike, it shows that some gentleman up there wrote a good hand.
That is a copy. The original is in the department.

My hon. friend states that his political opponent signed it. Of course he would sign it, any man would be a fool who would not ask for public money when he sees it being thrown around by the handful, and which the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton) the other night denounced. No wonder everybody in the neighbourhood says. When the money is going we might as well have a piece of it. The minister cannot defend this. He is going out of his way. I will be bound to say that Mr. Mackenzie is a political friend of the hon. gentleman.
I do not know him.
Well, the hon. member for North Grey knows him.
I do not know that he is any the worse for that, Mr. Chairman.

I am bound to say that If he was not a political friend, there would be no job and no proposition to buy his dock for $4,000. The whole country understands it. The minister says, Come along boys, all you who are political supporters of this government ; if you have not got a new dock to sell, then sell an old one. There is not an hon. gentleman on that side of the House who will rise in his place and denounce these jobs. The hon. member for Kingston had the temerity to do it the other night, but the lecture read to him by the Minister of Public Works was too much for him, and he has not opened his mouth since on this matter.

The hon. gentleman should have approached this question from a different direction. We are supplying wharfs to the farming, fishing and industrial communities, we are simply helping trade in this country, which is developing by leaps and bounds. The hon. gentleman finds fault with us. Well, I never was able to please him, and I really despair of being able to do so.

The disclosures this afternoon are rather a surprise to me. It apiiears that the government is adopting the policy of buying private docks in small harbours throughout the country. I remember well a few years ago, during the regime of the late government, it was thought desirable to have an old wharf improved and some dredging done in what was called a private harbour, because it belonged to one individual. The government of the day, however, replied that it could expend no money in such a case, that it could not expend money on a private harbour. In order to get an -appropriation of public money, the municipal council of the township went to the expense of purchasing this harbour to put themselves in a position to ask the government for a grant on the ground that it was public property. Now, I think it will be a surprise to my Liberal friends in the county of Halton, who went to the expense of purchasing this dock and this harbour, to find that in other counties friends of the government are more highly favoured, that their old docks are not only improved, but actually bought by the government. If the municipality of Trafalgar had known what the policy of the government was to be, they never would have gone to the expense of purchasing this old dock at Bronte on which the hon. minister is spending about $17,000, and with that I am finding no fault. I am very glad that I am to have a slice of these large expenditures in my own county.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) applied for this expenditure himself when his friends were in office.

Most assuredly, and I am telling the hon. gentleman the reason why I could not get it. I could not get it because it was not public property. It was owned by a private individual, and I told the people of the county that a grant could not be obtained because the government had not adopted the policy of granting money to improve private property.
The hon. gentleman applied anyway.

Friends of hon. gentlemen opposite took the matter up, and in order to make it a public property the municipal council acquired the property and then made an application. They were more successful than I was, on account of the greater liberality of the government. But, it will be rather a disappointment to these gentle-ment who have spent their own money in acquiring a private wharf, when they find that this government are not only improving private property of the same character as that wharf, but that they are actually buying it up and then improving it. I believe that the friends in my county have not been fairly dealt with.

I stated a while ago that I understood fairly well why these people were asking the hon. minister to shoulder the expense of a wharf and to take it over from Mackenzie. On the very petition itself the reason appears for it and it is this :
Your government in 1896 purchased Marksville dock from Elizabeth Duncan for $5,000; see Public Accounts, page 2, 157.
There is the reason assigned; it was because another party had been able to get $5,000 for a dock which it was a matter of notoriety in that neighbourhood was not worth one-half. It is refreshing to see the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce sit there in silent acquiescence with what is being done. There is not an hon. member on the other side of the House who will stand up and protest against these wharfs being bought with public money in order to provide for needy party friends. If so, so mote it be. Such things as these were quoted in North Bruce, and it is no wonder that the candidate of hon. gentlemen opposite was defeated.

North Bruce comes a little too often. The fight is over and my hon. friend has carried it. To speak seriously, I may say that wharfs were erected by private parties years ago and many of these works have gone into decay. It is necessary to have a wharf at this place. The requirements of trade demand it. Now, the government has to do one of two things, either buy the old property or build a new wharf. We are confronted with that state of affairs especially in Ontario, as I stated to the House last evening. A lot of works have
.5755

been erected in Ontario and they could not be kept up. The government have to decide whether they will construct new works or take over these old ones and repair them. My hon. friends always impute sinister motives. They say that we must please this friend or that. Of course, we are not here to displease our friends. We would be great fools indeed if we used our best endeavours to displease our friends. But when a question of this kind comes up it seems to me that it should be judged on its .jown merits.
Hear, hear.

Here is the question : Is it useful for the farming community to have a dock at this point ? I would say yes. Now the question is :	How much are we going to pay
for that property ? I stand here pledged to no price. If the gentleman asks too much I won't buy his property; that is all.

I stand by the view that I held at first in reference to this matter, and while I hold that view I do not charge that the hon. Minister of Public Works now is doing any differently from what has been done by other ministers in other parliaments all along the line, and therefore, what is the use of doing any more than simply . stating one's opinion in a matter of this kind ? I think it was a mistake that this private wharf was taken over by the government. It seems to me that while we all admit farmers need facilities for getting their produce to market, that they need good roads and need river transport, no government ought to be such a paternal gov. ernment that it would take charge of the private affairs of individuals and regulate them in that way. I think it is a mistake that the government has taken over private wharfs and maintained them at the public expense. I am not talking of one part of the Dominion any more than another, because I find that there has been a great deal of expenditure in Ontario in this direction. It seems to me to be a very difficult thing to stop it. Personally, I cannot see any reason why, when an individual builds a whai-f and it does not pay, that he should appeal to the government to take it off his hands and that it should be taken off his hands. In some cases it has been done, and I suppose will be done again, and all we can do about it is to enter one's protest. But I do not think it is fair, that being the state of affairs, to attempt to make political capital out of it.
Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Britton) state the cases that he refers to in which the late government purchased wharfs ?
I do not know any case in which they purchased wharfs, but I ; know cases in which they built them.
Where ?
I have a list of them.
I might refer to a case that I know of, but the hon. Minister of Public Works has a list of them.
The hon. gentleman stated that he knew of lots of similar cases in Ontario.
If I said that I only said what has been stated.
1 would ask the hon. gentleman to give a single case.

I will give a case. A wharf was built at the public expense in the village of Portsmouth near Kingston. This was under my own eyes, and that wharf has been maintained at public expense. Last year there was a sum in the estimates for repair. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) said, in reply to me, that at the time that wharf was built there was no penitentiary dock. I found out since that he was altogether mistaken in that. There was a penitentiary dock, and the wharf I mentioned has no connection with the penitentiary at all. It was built at the Portsmouth landing. There is a bay between the penitentiary and this wharf, which is built on the opposite side of that little bay. There is a government wharf that has been maintained at the public expense. Then, you may call it a lecture, it was rather a sharp rebuke that I got from the hon. Minister of Public Works, but as he had the facts on his side, perhaps he was quite right in saying what he did, and as he said it to me. I believe the fact to be so, that there were under former governments expenditures of this kind on new docks and for the purchase of docks from private owners which were maintained at the public expense or built at the public expense, and which have to be maintained. I think this was a mistake and I think it is a mistake to continue it, but I think it is unfair to the hon. Minister of Public Works to try to make political capital out of this when we find in the estimates such as we have here such large appropriations into* which, it does not seem, any polities enter at all. Even in a place so Conservative as Toronto when they are receiving consideration at the hands of the government, the members for that city attack the minister and try to make political capital out of it. It seems to me that it is carrying politics too far.

I differ altogether from what my hon. friend (Mr. Britton) has just said. I have not consented to buy wharfs because my predecessors did so. I was not actuated by any motive of that kind. Here is a place where a wharf is required for the farming and fishing community, and I will either have to buy the old wharf there or build a

new one. Where is the harm of buying the *old one if it costs less ? I don't see why I should apologize for carrying on a simple transaction. There is no use in apologizing ; apology is a bad business.

Public Works-Temporary clerical and other assistance, inclusive of services of all persons required who were first employed after July 1, 1882, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $11,000.
What is the reason of that-' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act ' ?
The reason is that we cannot pay for temporary employees a higher salary than $400. and, as my hon. friend knows, we cannot get skilled men for that amount of money.

But they all ought to pass the civil service examination unless they have some techniacl qualifiation ; and in that case the technical qualification should be mentioned and the vote taken separately. Here is a lump sum of $11,000, which will employ about twenty-five clerks.

)The same thing has been going on in my department for twenty years. The work

has increased so much that I cannot possibly carry it on with the same number of employees.

There are three items here together. The first is $11,000 for temporary, clerical and other assistance. Then there is $9,500 for salaries of the architects, draughtsmen and clerks in the chief architect's oflice. Then, in the chief engineer's office, there are the salaries of the engineers, draughtsmen and clerks, $9,500, making a total of $30,000, in addition to the main vote. That would mean fifty additional clerks, at an average salary of $600 each. What are the appropriations already for these three departments ?
Who is the chief engineer ?

Mr. Lafleur. He has not yet been permanently appointed chief engineer, as I like to try a man before entrusting him with a responsible position. When Mr. Coste resigned, Mr, Lafleur was next to him, and was appointed acting chief engineer. I began by increasing his salary, and increased it again a few months ago, which proves that I am satisfied with his services.

Three thousand dollars. He is not paid enough. He is a hard working man.

No, he is following his private avocations now.

Do these two items of $9,500 each represent the new temporary employees ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, No, there are some increases of salary. Mr. Routhier, the assistant architect, has had his salary increased by $500. Those men are often obliged to work at night.
Would it not be better to give reasonable salaries at once instead of increasing them every year ?

I did not know these officers when I took office, as I do now. When you have appreciated a man and know his work and give him an increase of salary, you encourage him. Mr. Routhier is a relatively young
man,	sober, active and trustworthy.

It seems to me improvident to make these men depend upon a yearly vote for the remuneration of their services. Would it not be better to fix their salaries instead of leaving them doubtful every year ?

So far as the heads of departments are concerned, it would be better to provide a large salary. The fixed salary of the chief engineer is $3,200. Mr. Lafleur only receives $3,000, although doing good work. He is
able,	sober, active and always ready. I am afraid he is not paid enough. My views may not be shared by everybody, but I feel that the good men are not paid as they ought to be. My hon. friend knows that in Montreal we could not get a first-class engineer for that amount of money.
None of these are on the superannuation list ?
No.

That has been the practice of all governments in Canada-to pay the men engaged on this 'scientific branch pretty fair wages, but without superannuation, and with the understanding that they are liable to dismissal at any time. It was thought that in that way we could get the most efficient people.

Has the minister had time to consider the case of Mr. Johnston, the military college engineer who died ? I see that no provision is made here for a gratuity. Also, has he had time to consider the case of the architect, Mr. New-Iands, to which I called attention some days ago ?

bnt they will be taken *Up as soon as possible.

Temporary, In a way. Most of them are professional men-architects, engineers or draughtsmen. By the way, if I could find some good draughtsmen, I should be glad.
