Public Works-Chargeable to Income-Chief Engineer's Office-Salaries of draughtsmen and clerks, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $9,500.
The minister was going to give us an explanation about this office. What amount was in the main estimates ?
In the main estimates there was an amount of $49,000, covering the salaries of resident engineers all over Canada.

I think the statement presented in the estimates is a very misleading one. It does not show that under these three heads of temporary assistants, chief architect's office and chief engineer's office, there are increases of salaries, wholesale increases. So, of course, we have no means of judging whether the increases are justifiable or not. But, one thing is clear, increases ought to follow some certain rule. In the main estimates, the amount voted for temporary clerical and other assistance was $25,000. and here, under these estimates, we have an additional amount of $11,000, making a total of $30,000. For the chief architect's office, the amount in the main estimates was $22,700, and now we have an addition of $9,500, or a total of $32,200. For the chief engineer's office, we voted, in the main estimates, $49,000, and here is an increase of $9,500, making a total of $58,500. That is to say, for the temporary assistance, engineering staff and architect's staff, we are voting a total of $126,700. For these three services we voted in the main estimates $96,000, and now we are adding over $30,000. This is on a par with the extravagant and wasteful expenditure of the government in every department of the public service. For clerical engineering and architect's staff, last year, we voted salaries of $96,700, which we may safely assume was a large increase over former years. And now we are adding over $30,000.

I ask my hon. friend to judge my department fairly; I hope he means to do so. When I took office, the expenditure under my de-181
partment-in 1896-reached only $1,600,000. For one reason or another, the department has been starved, to a very large extent. This year the budget in my department is $6,700,000, both capital and income. How could the heads of these offices be expected or asked to carry out their much heavier work with the staff they had four or five years ago ?
If a public building is being erected and an inspector is sent to it- I take it that the inspector's salary is taken from the appropriation for the building ?
Not always.
I think always. It is not included in the items we are voting here to-day ?
Yes. Take, for instance, Mr. Routhier, who is assistant architect-

The hon. minister does not understand me. I am speaking of an inspector who is to be on the ground inspecting a public building. Say, for instance, we are putting up a public building at Toronto Junction-though, I may say, I have no great expectations of it, and still less anxiety-the inspector there would be paid out of the appropriation for the building ?
Quite so.
Then, he is not paid out of this amount ? The plans are made out here, and these plans are charged against the building also ?
No, against this appropriation.
In every instance ?
Yes.
I understood that some of these expenses were charged against the works.
It may have happened, on very rare occasions, that an outside architect has been employed, but, as a rule, the cost of preparing the plans for a public building comes out of this appropriation.
The hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart), who has more practical knowledge of the working of the construction departments, says that very often that is done.
Not in my department.
Yes.
Very rarely.

Perhaps not lately, but often It has been done. The bon. gentleman will remember the celebrated case of the Prince Edward Island wharfs where even two or three pistols were charged to the construction of the wharf, and the expenses of the party going down there, and there was no wharf built at all.

Amount required for trails, roads and bridges, Yukon territory, $70,000.

It will be necessary to make a statement, not at very great length, but still at some length to have the matter thoroughly understood. The total amount voted by parliament is as follows : In 1899-1900, $175,000, and in 1900-1901, $50,000, making a total of $225,000. In the main estimates passed in committee this year, there is a further sum of $40,000 for the next fiscal year. These amounts have been disposed of as follows : In the summer of 1899, Mr. McCarthur, an old surveyor employed in the Department of the Interior was despatched to the Yukon on the recommendation of the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) for the purpose

of improving the winter road between Bennett and Dawson. He spent on that work $17,750. He started his work from a point at the foot of Lake LeBarge touching the Nordenskiold river at some point a little below Five Finger Rapids. During the same year the Department of the Interior informed the Department of Public Works that Mr. Ogilvie had expended in making the roads in the Klondike district, in the vicinity of Dawson, $90,000, and they asked us that the sum be defrayed out of tne appropriation of $175,000 that has been voted by parliament. This was agreed to, but the accounts were not in proper shape at the end of the fiscal year so that only $70,000 of the $96,000 could be paid out of the appropriation. In 1900, while I was away, but 1 quite approve of the decision taken then, it was decided to place an engineer of the Department of Public Works in charge of the road-making, and Mr. Tache was sent out there. Out of the appropriation he spent $15,000, so that the total amount expended out of the sum voted for the year 1899-1900 was as follows : Expenditure of Mr. Me-Carthur, $17,750 ; expenditure of the Department of the Interior, $70,000 ; expenditure of Mr. TachC, $15,000. In other words, the total expenditure was $102,750. The sum of $72,250 lapsed, because the accounts, as I said, were not in shape at the end of the fiscal year. For the year 1900-1901, $50,000 was voted with an expenditure up to date of $32,000, leaving a balance of $18,000 which will be spent up to the 30th of June, making then a total expenditure of $70,000 by the Department of the Interior ; $64,750 by the Department of Public Works, or a grand total of $134,750. For this year the Department of Public Works are asking $40,000 in the main estimates and $70,000 in the supplementary estimates. The Department of the Interior have sent us an account of the expenditure made by Mr. Ogilvie amounting to a little over $94,000, that sum being made up of $26,000 of expenditure made in 1899-1900, the accounts for which could not be put in shape for the end of the fiscal year, and about $68,000 for the actual expenditure made during the last year by Mr. Ogilvie without reference to any authority of the Public Works Department. In other words, the Local Council spent $68,000 in the way I have just stated, placing us under the obligation of asking $80,000 to reimburse the Local Council for the money they have advanced and of asking for $110,000 to be spent under the direction of the Department of Public Works on the following roads. Perhaps those of my hon. friends who take an interest in the Yukon would like to look at a map of the roads which have been built in the past and of the roads that are to be built. The roads that have been built in the past are represented by the plain lines. The roads that are to be built with the $110,000 that I am asking are represented by the 1811
dotted lines. I may say that the roads proposed to be built have been approved by Mr. Tache and Mr. Girouard, an employee of the Local Council. The roads proposed to be built are the following :
From Dawson to Hunker, about 8 miles.
From Hunker to Summit, about 20 miles.
From Summit to Dominion Creek, about 4 miles.
From Dominion Creek up to 75 below Lower Discovery, 10 miles.
On Last Chance Creek, 5 miles.
From 30 Eldorado to Quartz Creek, 8 miles.
On Quartz Creek, 6 miles.
On Sulphur Creek, 10 miles.
From Gold Run to Clear Creek, 39 miles.
Along Bonanza from Grand Forks to Ridge road, 12 miles.
Making a total of 122 miles. All these roads have been approved by Mr. Girouard who discussed the question with the Department of Public Works, and by Mr. Tache, the engineer of the Public Works Department there.

After the lucid explanation which the hon. minister has given, which I am sure not a single member of this House could follow intelligently to ascertain how the amounts are accounted for, I suppose we will have to vote this sum, but it looks to me like voting $164,000' without a knowledge of what it is for. How much of this amount will be expended upon these roads ?

I am asking this year $110,000 for 122 miles of road. This time I will know where the money will go. I have wired the new commissioner, Mr. Ross, that the Department of Public Works or the government will not stand one cent of expenditure that will not be authorized first. I do not want to recriminate or blame anybody, but I am obliged to ask parliament this year for $80,000 for roads over which the Department of Public Works had no control. They simply made the roads and the accounts came in and we had to pay them. That will not happen again. I wired the new commissioner that I will not ask parliament to vote a dollar for roads that have not been built under the control of the department.
The minister knew nothing about the $80,000 until it was spent ?
I did not know a word about it. The council presided over by Mr. Ogilvie built the roads, and we had to pay.
That is the way our money goes.

I think the roads are built all right, but all the same It must not occur again.

speechtext: The Post Office Department pays this amount, but objection has been taken to the two departments paying for the service.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: In estimating the expenditure of the Post Office Department, how do you do with the subsidies to mail steamers ?

They are charged as separate votes. The reason for that is that in a great many cases, although the mails are bound to be carried, the mail subsidy is to a great extent a subsidy for freight service for the purpose of encouraging general communication. In this case the Post Office saves, and this department will have to pay the whole service.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I would like to ask the minister if the large subsidy for carryiug the mails to Great Britain is charged to the Post Office Department ?

It has never been charged to the mail service. Of course, while it is desirable, and has always been held iso by both parties for a long time, to maintain a mail service from Canadian ports to Great Britain, the great bulk of our mail from the very necessity of the case, goes by New York and other American ports, from which there is an almost daily service, and a faster service than ours, and we cannot refuse to our merchants the right of communicating by that. The consequence is that only an insignificant portion of the Canadian mail matter goes by our weekly service. It is perhaps a service which should be charged against the Post Office Department.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Are none of these mail subsidies and steamship subventions charg-able against the Post Office Department ?

None; but the Post Office Department in some cases pays an extra sum.

The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Have the government been doing anything lately towards securing a fast Atlantic service, or has that matter dropped out of their category of business ?

No, it has not by any means; but, as the hon. gentleman knows, times have been very unpropitious until now for entering into any new contracts. The cost of building steamships during the last two or three years has increased so much as to be almost prohibitory; but the subject is engaging our attention, and at the present time some negotiations are going on upon the subject, though they are not in a state to enable me to make any positive statement to the House. I may mention one thing; that is, that the enormous increase in the cost of coal is a very serious consideration in the estimate of cost for this service. I am not quite certain how much it amounts to, but certainly the cost of coal is now 50 per cent or 60 per cent more than it was three or four years ago; and in the case of vessels expecting to traverse the ocean at any great speed, that is an enormous factor in the possible cost of a voyage. However, the subject has been by no manner of means abandoned, and it may be, though I cannot venture to say positively, that in the course of the next two or three months we shall be in a position to obtain some reasonable offers. The House is aware that the concurrence of the British government is necessary on this subject, that is, if we are to obtain the benefit of the offer which was at one time made to us, and we are at the present moment negotiating with them on the subject.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
I hope the hon. gentleman will see toy this time the mistake this government made in cancelling the contract which was entered into by their predecessors. I have no doubt that they have seen it many times since; but I think a good many people will agree that we are losing ground every season that we are without a faster and better trans-Atlantic service. It seems to me that the trade is going by the United States, and we are making that country a thoroughfare for both passengers and products from this country; and I think
we cannot avail ourselves a moment too soon of any opportunity we can have of getting both a faster and a better Atlantic service than we have at the present time.

I may remind my hon. friend that the contract to which he refers was anything but a fair contract. The Allans never made an offer which satisfied us. That matter has been discussed a great many times in the House; but I must protest against it being supposed that the offer was to be considered a fair offer.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I believe we shall never have a satisfactory fast Atlantic service until we build our own steamships. I believe we could build at a comparatively small cost two fast steamers which would be sufficient for a beginning. They do not so much need to be very large as they do to be modern and up-to-date. I believe there are men who would go into such a proposition. I believe there are men in Halifax and in Cape Breton who are considering it, and the sooner we start doing our own ship-building in this country the better for ourselves. As to the dearer coal, that is due to the enormous combine which has sprung up in the United States, and which has taken possession of the railways and some of the Atlantic liners, and are controlling the coal fields of the United States. It is also said that they are controlling the coal fields of Canada and dictating the price at which they will sell the coal. To fight that combine this country will have to build its own steamships and perhaps own its own coal fields.

and experienced artisans, and it would take some considerable time before the plant could be put in such a position that a tender could be made. I do not desire to throw cold water on any proposition for constructing steamships of the largest capacity and best description on this side, if it can be done, and there is reasonable ground for the hope that the works now being started at Sydney will ultimately be so developed as to bring this within the range of reasonable probability.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
If the hon. minister would let it be known in England that the Canadian government is prepared to negotiate with any large shipbuilding firm from the Clyde, Tyneside, or Belfast, and give reasonable encouragement, it is very probable that one of these large firms would transfer a portion of its establishment to Canada, and be able to build this class of steamships in a very short time.
We have given protection to steel plates, and I believe that we will be manufacturing plates at several places in Canada, and now is the time to advertise that we are prepared to offer inducements to some great shipbuilding enterprise to transfer its works from the old country to Canada. I believe that such an announcement ought to be made and that some kind of a response would come which would end in Canada having, in a year or two, a first-class shipbuilding industry. We have the iron, and the coal, and the capital, and we need the ships. The only satisfactory transatlantic service that Canada will ever have will be one which will be controlled on this side of the Atlantic, and which we will be in a position to use for the development of our Canadian ports. I urge this on the ground of national policy, and because what other governments have done we can do. Germany has built up one of the largest marines in the world, although the Germans were not a shipbuilding people, and had no marine engineers. But through the protection given this industry, the German establishments are turning out the largest ships in the world. All we require is confidence in ourselves, and if we announce a policy of assisting the establishment of such an industry, I have no doubt that some of the great shipbuilding firms will take advantage of our offer.

I agree most heartily in what the hon. gentleman has said, as to the desirability of our utilizing this great contract-if we are to make one-as an instrument in assisting the establishment of a great shipbuilding industry in this country. I have given considerable attention to that policy myself. While no formal negotiations have taken place which can be submitted to parliament, I have taken pains to see that great shipbuilding companies in the old country have been communicated with on the subject. Intimation has been given them that if any Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
one of them would approach this government with a proposal, they would find the government ready to give every possible consideration to it. I have had some conversations with gentlemen connected with very great enterprises of the kind in the old country, and while willing to consider the idea they rather estimate the difficulties in the way as more serious than my hon. friend does. People speak of the building of a steel steamer sometimes as if the great consideration was the making of the steel plate, whereas the steel plates are only a very moderate proportion of the total cost. The real difficulty is in assembling the material, especially the machinery, and also in the Importation of a large amount of skilled labour. The difficulties of that character are much greater than those connected with the production of steel plates. The latter we will overcome in a very short time. I am only too pleased to find my hon. friend taking the view Hie does of this matter. If we are to give this contract to any company, and that company is disposed, at a small advance, to undertake to build the ships in Canada, we would be disposed to give such a proposition every consideration. And I may say that while we have had no formal negotiations, the matter has not been overlooked, and a proposition of that kind may yet be submitted.

We should all rejoice if the building of ships out of steel in Nova Scotia and other provinces should become a great industry. The building of wooden ships was a very great industry with us, but owing to the changed conditions, that is now largely a thing of the past. Men who are familiar with steel shipbuilding tell me that the character of the work is to some extent the same, and that the artisans employed in the building of wooden ships in Nova Scotia, would be very apt men in the building of steel ships. I would regard it as rather a large undertaking to begin the business of shipbuilding in our country by the construction of steamers such as are suitable for the fast Atlantic line, but if it can be done, I hope those steamers may be built in our own country instead of on the other side.
Referring to what was said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce a few moments ago, there cannot be much doubt that if this government had persevered in the policy adopted by the late government, we would have had a fast Atlantic service before now. But, instead, this government cut off $250,000 from the annual grant, reducing the-grant from $750,000 to $500,000, and the Imperial government made a like reduction.
They made a contract for $500,000, but the grant was not reduced.

It really amounts to the same thing. The contract made with Petersen, Tate & Co. called for $500,000 a-

year, and the Imperial government were to give $250,000 per year. The proposal made to the Allans was $750,000 by our government, and one-half that amount by the Imperial authorities. The result of the policy of the present government was that we did not get the fast Atlantic service at all. It is somewhat amusing to look back at the debates of 1807-8, and read the assurances of the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dobell), that the opposition should really be very much ashamed of themselves when they observed the tremendous success which had attended the efforts of this government, which was providing a splendid service at a cost of $250,000 per year less than that offered by the previous government.
He almost made us, on this side, feel ashamed of ourselves when he explained what a magnificent bargain it was, and what an assured success. And we had the same intimation from the right hon. leader of the House. And month after month, and year after year, this went on. The first boat. I think, was to have crossed the Atlantic in 1899, and all of them were to be built before the end of 1900. This is 1901, and the keels are not yet laid. More than that, the enterprise has been completely abandoned. Now, perhaps it is not of much use to talk about that-it is passed and cannot be helped. But, it may be useful for the good of my hon. friends opposite, as showing that when they depart from a policy laid down by their predecessors, they are apt to go wrong-and they certainly have gone very wrong in this case. If they had persevered in the policy of the Conservative administration, no doubt, we should have had a fast Atlantic service by this time. More than that, as suggested by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, even If we get the fast Atlantic service now, the cost of building ships is very much increased.
It is diminishing very rapidly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I understood that it was diminishing, but I did not know that it was diminishing very rapidly. Is it yet down to the figure at which it stood in 1896 ?
I do not think so, but it may be.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: It may get down to that. I hope it will. For, the more the price diminishes the better our prospects are. But, it seems to me that when, eventually, we do get this fast Atlantic service, the country will find it necessary to revert to the policy of the late Conservative government, which, when it was presented to this House, if my memory serves me right, was unanimously approved by parliament. I trust that the negotiations which the Minister of Trade and Commerce says are being carried on with regard to this matter will result in something satisfactory at an early day, for I believe it to be of very great importance to this country as a whole-not alone to the maritime provinces and Quebec, but to the whole Dominion-that this service should be upon a proper footing at the earliest possible moment.

If I say a word or two on this subject, it will not be to follow exactly the line of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax). I think there are questions which may, with great advantage, be discussed without bringing in particularly the political aspect of the matter. I feel that we are entirely of one opinion in this parliament-and I think the same might be said by the country at large as to the importance and desirability of pursuing a policy that will, at an early day, result in the construction of steel ships in Canada. In my own constituency, I am glad to say, the subject is arousing a great deal of active interest among men who are large owners of ships, and who have established a very successful line of ships for ordinary freight purposes, but who are prepared to devote their energies toward the organization of a company which shall take up in earnest the subject of ship-building in the maritime provinces. I know, from frequent conversation with the gentlemen who are identified with, the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, that they are not anxious to aid and encourage such an enterprise as one of the branches incident to their undertaking. Some of these gentlemen have been in close communication with the parties I have indicated in the city of St. John. There are very good grounds for entertaining the hope that these people will succeed in establishing a ship-building industry in that city. The gentlemen I have indicated are, as I have said, already the owners of some ten or twelve ships which, of course, have been built on the other side of the water. But. with their knowledge of the subject, and with the feeling which exists among the people in the maritime provinces, that ship-building is an industry entirely in keeping with their instincts and training, they are confident that, with some encouragement from the government, at the outset. at all events, of the undertaking, they will be able to put such an industry upon a successful footing. My hon. friend from East York, who has espoused this matter so jealously, may rest assured that the matter is not going to escape the attention of the government. There are many who are very anxious, indeed, that energetic steps should be taken in order that it may not be many days before we may have a shipbuilding industry in this country. I think it will be a rather ambitious commencement to undertake the construction of such ships as we would hope to have arranged for in connection with the fast line from Canada. I think that a company, to be

successful, would need to start in a more modest way, and that it would be more certain to establish ultimately a prosperous business if it were so to start. I think that everybody who has thought on the subject recognized the extreme difficulty of securing the construction of the necessary machinery in Canada for some time to come. They would only hope to construct the hulls and other Incidental portions of the ship, and would look to procuring the machinery very largely in the old country. In common with my hon. friend, I hope that we may, at an early day, pride ourselves upon the establishment in Canada of such an industry as he has referred to.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Just another word, Mr. Chairman. While I agree with a great deal of what the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) has said, the point is this- the empire is growing, and the thing that is manifest now is, that an industry is as valuable to the empire if it is in Canada as if it is in the mother land. Once the great capitalists of Great Britian see that they can carry on their industry in Canada as well as in the mother country, they would be willing to transfer that industry to Canada. They will bring their shops and yards here. The plates for steamers designed for the fast Atlantic service can be rolled here. For the first one or two, we may bring the engines from the old country-
I do not know why.

Well, for a start, we might have an engine or two built there. But, if an existing ship-building firm brings its industry here, it will be able to build engines of the largest kind. There is no reason why that cannot be done. It will be done if the statement goes abroad that the parliament of Canada is prepared to encourage some large shipyard now in the old countiy to transfer its industry to this side of the Atlantic.

I am heartily in accord with the idea that this country should have a fa'St Atlantic service. I am also in accord with the idea that this country, if it is to have a fast Atlantic service, must have that service in connection with the government system of railways. I believe that it is not too ambitious a project to undertake here the building of large steamers. In my own town of Sydney, the material for the construction of such steamers can be brought together more conveniently than in any other part of the world. And I may say that from a gentleman of Sydney, who is now in England interviewing large firms of ship-builders to induce them to come over and look at the site, I am perfectly satisfied, and every hon. gentleman who knows the situation will be Mr. BLAIR.
satisfied, that Sydney presents to ship builders opportunities which should induce some of them to remove from the old country and establish themselves there. The materials are there, and it is not at all too ambitious a project for this Dominion to entertain.
Additional for direct steam communication between Prince Edward Island and Great Britain, $5,000.

The House will recollect there was a vote of $5,000 granted for this purpose. That has been found too small to secure anything like adequate steam communication, and the vote is therefore asked to be increased to $10,000. With that I think we will be able to obtain six trips during the season of navigation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman concluded a contract with any firm of shipowners ?
We are negotiating with them now. We have considerable difficulty owing to the fact that we had only $5,000 to offer. Now that we have $10,000, I think we will be able to secure a reasonable service.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I remember that three months ago the hon. gentleman said they were negotiating with a firm for tne Prince Edward Island service.
We have not been able to assign a contract yet.	>
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Now is the time that the people require this accommodation.
They will get it when this vote is passed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I trust the hon. gentleman will see his way at once to conclude a contract.
I am taking the best means to do it, getting $10,000 instead of $5,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I am glad to see that parliament is ready to vote this money. It will be said in Prince Edward Island that the government of Canada is endeavouring to do them a small measure of justice.

I think it has done some justice to Prince Edward Island.
For a semi-weekly service between Halifax and Canso during the season of navigation, $4,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.
The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Will they carry the mails ?

I do not think there will be much mail service done by these boats, but what mail there is will be carried by them.
For a winter steam navigation service between Quebec and the St. Lawrence harbours down to Murray Bay and Riviere Ouelle, $12,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OP TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: I suppose this is to test the navigability of the St. Lawrence in winter ?

That is largely the intention. A vote of $5,000 'was struck out of the main estimates in order to replace it by this sum. We found that $5,000 was of no use for the purpose of obtaining a winter service. We may have to get a boat built for the service.	.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Will you be able to get one in time for navigation during the coming winter ?
1 am informed that the parties concerned hope to be able to supply one.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Is the experiment limited to the route between Quebec and Murray Bay anid Riviere Ouelle ?
If that is found to be navigable during the winter, I am informed it will go a long way towards solving the problem of winter navigation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Then, it is not intended to go further down at present ? Will there be regular service between Quebec and those places, so far as practicable, during the winter ?

That is our intention. The hou. gentleman knows there is a large population to be served by that, we have no communication otherwise.
Administration of Justice-Supreme Court of Canada-To provide for one second-class clerk, R. G. Davis, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $1,100.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: What is the reason of fixing the salary notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act ?

Mr. Davis is secretary to the judges of the Supreme Court. The intention is to permit him to go, without examination, from the position of a third-class clerk to that of a second-class clerk. He is secretary and stenographer to the judges of the Supreme Court.
To provide for the appointment of a judge of the Court of Divorce and Matrimonial Causes in New Brunswick, $500.

What has the Solicitor General to say in regard to voting money Cor divorce courts in one province and not supplying them in others ? We had that question up the other day. If) the Dominion is paying money to establish a divorce court, or to assist in maintaining one, in New Brunswick, why should he not give similar jurisdiction to maintain a similar court in the province of Ontario, and thus avoid the scandals that have been going on in connection with divorce cases in the Senate ?

I would remind the hon. gentleman that we are not establishing a divorce court. In the province of New Brunswick there is one in existence, and has been since previous to confederation. The intention is merely to provide for a payment of $500 to the judge who presides over that court, and who heretofore has done so without remuneration.

You should do the same thing for Ontario.
Administration of Justice in the Yukon Territory-Additional amount required for maintenance of prisoners, $20,000.
We had a large amount in the main estimates for that purpose.

This will make $40,000 for that purpose. It is represented that it costs $2 per day to maintain the prisoner in that country. These amounts are paid out by the North-west Mounted Police and charged against the Department of Justice and we refund them. In order to justify the amount I may say that the average daily number of prisoners in that part of the country is 52. My hon. friend can estimate the cost of maintaining 52 prisoners daily for 365 days in the year and he will find that it amounts to something over the amount that we are asking for.

I think this is a good territory in which to provide for the ticket-of-leave system. It is far better to ship these men out of the country than to pay $1,000 each to retain them.
Gas and Electric Light Inspection-Further sum required to enable the department to purchase necessary electrical instruments for head office for standardizing purposes, $2,600.

It seems to me with the large number of new electric light plants

that we are having established all over the country there is need of some independent inspection, because I am quite satisfied that municipal corporations and individuals who are obliged to use this light are frequently not getting what they agree to get when they enter into their contract. They may stipulate for a 16-candle power, or a 32-candle power, but it is very often much below what it is represented to be. How often does an inspection of electric light take place ?

Once in five years, but at any time the consumer or the contractor may ask the government inspector to inspect his meter. As I explained the other day, the party in default has to bear the expense, ranging from 75 cents to $2 per light. This item is to enable us to get instruments which are to be bought on the requisition of the electrical engineer in order to perfect the system of inspection.
speakername: The MINISTER OF INLAND REVENUE (Hon. M. E. Bernier).

speechtext:
There are two classes of meters. There may be a meter at a private dwelling and in another case there is no meter at the private dwelling at all, but the meter, if any, is at the place where the plant is located. If it is found that the lights are not up to the requirements, and complaint is made, how would the person complaining secure the services of the inspector ? Would the individual or the municipality, be able to have an inspection at any time ?
The	MINISTER	OF	INLAND	REV-
ENUE. Any party interested, the contractor, or the consumer, or the municipality, may ask for an inspection.

And the party who asks for the inspection must pay the cost of it ?
The	MINISTER	OF	INLAND	REVENUE.	The party	in default.Mr.	SPROULE.	How	often are	these
meters inspected ?

Once in five years, but any party interested may ask for the services of a government inspector, but the official inspection takes places once in five years.
Inspection of Staples-Additional sum required to pay salaries of chief inspectors, inspectors and other employees under the General Inspection Act and the Manitoba Grain Act, $35,000.

The reason why this sum is required is that it is proposed to pay the chief inspector and the assistant inspectors by salaries and not by fees, and that such fees be refunded to the credit of the consolidated fund. The fees of the inspection, we think, will equal the expenditure, this sum being simply an advance.
What is to be the salary of the chief inspector ?
It is not yet fixed.
Has the hon. gentleman no idea what it is to be ?
We cannot tell. It will be $3,000 or $4,000, I suppose.

I believe it is proposed to appoint a number of additional inspectors. How many Inspectors have you now, how many more do you propose to appoint, and if it is agreeable, could the hon. gen-, tleman tell us whom he intends to appoint ?

We have no inspectors under the disposition of the new Act which was passed last week. We propose to appoint as many inspectors and sub-inspectors as are required by the trade. There will be one chief inspector, and an inspector in every locality, where the services of these inspectors are required. Those _ appointed now are in Manitoba under a different Act, but these officers mentioned here are to be appointed throughout the Dominion outside of Manitoba where the system of inspection is regulated by another Act. These appointments are to be made under the terms of the new Act. We do not know how many officers will be required for the service. There will be one at St. John, Halifax, Quebec, Montreal, Toronto, and perhaps some other places, but the amount of the salary is not fixed, and the number of these officers is not determined.

You would not say what the salary will be ?
The	MINISTER	OF	INLAND	REV-
ENUE. No, the chief inspector will have about $3,000 or $4,000 a year salary.

Where will he be located ?
The	MINISTER	OF	INLAND	REV-
VENUE. Probably in Montreal, and there will be inspectors in several other places such as Toronto, Quebec, Halifax, St. John, &c.

What qualifications will these inspectors have ?
The	MINISTER	OF	INLAND	REV-ENUE. They have already passed^ an examination before a board of examiners at the Boards of Trade in Toronto and Montreal.	These examinations have	taken
place in both cities within the last few weeks. A board of examiners was chosen, and the private individuals who applied for the position of inspectors were required to pass an examination, some in Toronto and some in Montreal.
Will the results of the examination be made public-the percentage of marks obtained by those who went up for examination ?
No, the marks are not generally given, but the board issue a certificate to those who have qualified themselves.
Will these selections be made out of those who have passed this examination, or are these positions to be open to others as well ?

Others may be examined later on. The examination has been held at intervals in order to be ready to put this Act into operation. These examinations have taken place in Montreal and Toronto, and I suppose that among those who have passed the examination the government can make a selection.
Will you chose the candidates who have obtained the largest number of marks ?
I cannot say that ; I do not know.

Is it proposed that the chief inspector shall be selected from among those who are already in the service, and have been for long periods, or is it proposed that the selection shall be made from outside the service ? I ask that question because experience is of very great value in so important a work as this. A man of long training and experience would necessarily render more important service to the country.
The selections can be made from among those who have passed the examination, or those who have been grain inspectors in the past, or from amongst those who have passed their examinations recently-
I have asked the hon. gentleman if a selection is likely to be made from among those who are engaged in the service at present ?

I cannot tell, because no selection has been made.

\	Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
To pay the representatives of the late senator, Hon. J. J. Ross, who died during the session of 1901, the amount of his indemnity, $1,000.

I beg to move that the following words be added to that item : ' Payment to be made to such person as the Treasury Board may determine.' The explanation of that is that sometimes there is a question as to the person legally entitled to receive these moneys, and it is thought best that instead of placing
them in the estate they should be disposed of as the Treasury Board thinks best.
What about the increased indemnity ?

That will have to be settled afterwards.
Senate-Further amount required for salaries, $3,226.
What is this for ?
All l can say is that the Senate decided to increase the salaries of some of its employees and it did not consult the House.
Can they do it that way 7
They cannot do it unless the government put in an item in the estimates to cover it.
I suppose you want to live on good terms with the Senate ?

As a matter of fact they did pay the money out of their general credit vote, and the Auditor General took exception to it.
To provide for hydrographic survey of Lake Winnipeg, $10,000.

There is no chart of any kind of Lake Winnipeg, and the consequence is that it is impossible at present to get insurance for vessels plying on that lake. The Minister of Marine estimates the total cost of the survey at $25,000, and he asks this $10,000 on account.
Have you a tug there to make the survey ?

I do not know what the arrangements of the Minister of Marine are to carry on the work, but it is possible one of the Public Works tugs may be utilized. If the tugs are too busy a small vessel can be hired.
North-west Territories-Additional amount to schools, $25,000.

I have here a statement which shows that the payments of the North-west Territories government on account of school grants have increased to such an extent that this year the increase over last year amounts to over $20,000. The large number of foreign settlers going into the Territories makes it imperative that some special assistance should be given for the purpose of establishing a system of education amongst them. This is for the purpose of enabling the North-west government to do that.
What do we pay the North-west government for the maintenance of schools ?

We do not pay them anything specially for

tlie maintenance of schools. We pay them a lump sum in the same way as we pay the provincial subsidies.
What is the usual amount ?
In the main estimates it is $332,979. It is described as ' grant for schools, clerical assistance, printing, &c.'
Have they a system of free schools ?

Yes, and on account of the sparseness of settlement it is necessary to give them a larger grant than would be the case if the settlements were closer together, and they were able to help themselves more by local taxation.
For the equipping and maintaining of an assay office in British Columbia or Yukon territory. $20,000.
I notice that in one of the papers it was stated that there was a proposal to establish three or four assay offices. Is there to be only one, or more than one ?

I notice that one of the British Columbia papers suggested that it would be a profitable investment to establish three or four offices, but no decision has been reached as yet to establish more than one. The question whether there should be one in Dawson and one in British Columbia, is worthy of consideration. Certainly, we do not propose to establish more than two, and probably only one. This vote is to provide for one.
To provide for expenses of a judicial inquiry into alleged paper combine, $3,000.
Does this cover the expense of witnesses ?

Some witnesses will be paid out of this vote ; but so far as our determination as to the manner of conducting the investigation is this : The gentlemen who made the complaint intimated their willingness to make out their case, and we think they should be permitted to do so. As respects witnesses and counsel, they will make their own arrangements. The parties on the other side will do likewise ; but if the judge in his discretion should wish to call other witnesses, we think he should be free to do so, and the cost of all witnesses summoned by him will be paid out of this vote.	4
Will the inquiry be held at one place ?
The inquiry will be held in the first place by the judge at Montreal ; but, if necessary, he will be free to hold it anywhere else. That is a matter on which we have given no instructions.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Will the government be represented at the inquiry ?
At present we do not think it necessary. We will watch the inquiry, but we think there will be a strong contest between the two sides, which will bring out the truth.

You think the public will be sufficiently represented by the judge and the people who make out the
case ?

Yes, we think so. This is the first ease of the kind.
Astronomical Observatory-For purchase of telescope and apparatus, $15,000.

We took an appropriation for the purchase of a telescope a couple of years ago, but there was no appropriation that year for an observatory. We are now taking an appropriation for the construction of a small observatory besides this vote.
Have you decided yet what telescope you will purchase, and the size of it ?

No, not positively. The chief astronomer suggested at the time we took the appropriation before that a telescope with a 10-inch lens would probably answer the purpose. That would probably cost $6,000 or $7,000. But, we now think a larger one will be necessary.
I think it would be a great mistake to put up a small one, or one that would not be acceptable at the capital of the country.
What is the practical object of this expenditure ?

It is absolutely necessary to check the work; of the Surveyor General's Department by astronomical observation. As I said when I explained the previous item, I do not think that anything is more disgraceful to the government service than the way in which the astronomical work is compelled to be carried on, with practically no accommodation at all.

I do not think it will be of any practical value at the present time to have a lens of less than twelve inches ; and a first-class optician ought to be consulted, so as to get the latest results of science. I would suggest that the government might confer with the firm of Alvin Clark, in New York, or Grubb & Son, in Dublin, who would be able to supply the most approved glasses.

I may say that the chief astronomer of the department, Mr. King, has been in con-consultation with Mr. Clark's people, and the work will be done by them if possible.

Census-Additional amount required, $100,000.

I may say that the Minister of Agriculture has departed and is not able to present this item himself. He informed me, however, when leaving, that it would be necessary to obtain this further appropriation. It does not mean any additional cost for the taking of the census ; but the returns are coming-in so rapidly that it is believed that the work can be finished in a shorter time than was anticipated. Consequently, it is deemed necessary to take this further appropriation for a larger staff.	.
Can the minister tell us when* he will have the population returns ?
And what is he going to do about the census enumerators who are grumbling about their pay ?

It will probably be July or August before we shall have the population returns. As to the other question, the minister has already made a statement to the House to the effect that there was a misunderstanding on the part of some of the officials-that they -were not going to be paid so small a sum as they had imagined, but were to be paid on a very liberal scale. It is piecework, but I think it is all that the parties themselves expected.

I am told by some of them that that was not their opinion of it, and they were threatening vengeance on the government if they did not get $3 a day. I think some of them went so far as to say that they would sue the government.

Perhaps the minister can give us a little further information. The statement is very commonly made throughout the country, that on the authority of enumerators, the population of a certain village is so much, and of another it is so much. I would like to ask the hon. minister if the enumerators are permitted to give out the figures, showing the population of any particular place. I have always understood that they were not permitted to give out any information before furnishing it to the government.

The hon. gentleman's view of the law and practice is quite right. No enumerator is at liberty to give information. If he has done so, he has done it in violation of the instructions, and, I think I may say, of his oath.

The difficulty about the pay of the enumerators is that it will work very hard in cities and towns and work out all right in the rural municipalities. There was a general understanding, I think authorized by the instructions, that the enumerators were to get $3 a day. To pay according to the number of names would suit in the rural municipalities, especially
where each enumerator is allowed a horse and can use his own horse to go around, but in cities and towns, especially where the ward is small, the pay will be very little and there will be a good deal of grumbling. What is the settlement arrived at ?

There is nothing to be said except to refer to the circular issued to the commissioners, who -were instructed to explain to the enumerators what was intended to be the remuneration. I hope the enumerators will find that they have been needlessly alarmed and that they will earn $3 per day. There may be eases in which the returns will not give that amount, but it is fully expected that the enumerators will be able to earn that sum if they are at all active.
Some resolutions reported.

Bill (No. 146) to authorize the granting of subsidies in aid of the construction of the lines of railway therein mentioned (Hon. Mr. Blair) read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.

I may say in explanation of this Bill that it is introduced for the purpose of defining the meaning of the word ' facilities ' in section 240 of the Railway Act. We have had occasion, in interpreting that Act, which confers powers upon the Railway Committee, to enforce the granting of facilities by one railway company to another, or by one company having connection with another company, whether a steamship line or a railway line, and the question of what the word ' facilities ' actually means, has given rise to a good deal of controversy before the committee. Section 240 of the Railway Act was almost identical with a similar clause in the English Railway Act, when it was adopted, or as it was enforced at the time when our Railway Act passed. But subsequently to that period, the same difficulties and troubles have arisen, I presume, which we have found to arise in interpreting the meaning of the word, and the English parliament amended their Railway Act. We are now proposing to amend ours practically in the same direction, not adopting the same precise language, because the conditions which exist in England are not identical with the conditions which exist here. In order that we might avoid the pitfalls which are constantly liable to be encountered when you undertake to deal with traffic matters without full knowledge, we have given notice to the larger and more important railway companies in this country, sending them a copy of our original draft, and asking them to confer with us in respect of the proposed Bill. They have done so. We have had a good deal of debate with them, a good deal of discussion, and the result of the conferences which have taken place is that we have agreed upon the clause as it is now presented to the committee. Before the resolution is concurred in, I wish to ask the right hon. the Prime Minister, if any conclusion has been reached by the government with respect to giving aid to Capt. Bernier for his expedition to the North Pole ? That is a matter in Which members on both sides take a deep interest. In committee, a very inconclusive statement was made regarding the attitude of the government, and I now ask the right hon. gentleman if it is the intention of the government to give some aid to Captain Bernier, who I believe is a worthy man and well deserving of assistance, to enable him to proceed with his expedition to the North Pole ?

The government has come to no conclusion with regard to the expedition of Capt. Bernier to the North Pole.	The government has not
thought it advisable to ask parliament to vote any appropriation this session. I understand, from information supplied to me personally and I believe supplied to members of the House generally, by Capt. Bernier himself, that he expects his contemplated expedition would cost in the neighbourhood of $120,000. Capt. Bernier has asked the government to give $60,000, or half the cost. I repeat that the government has not thought fit to ask parliament for this appropriation ; not that the government would not be disposed to contribute generously to such an object as that, but the government did not think it would serve any good purpose to vote any sum to Capt. Bernier unless there was some reasonable expectation that the balance of the money required would be contributed. I have no authority at this

moment to speak for the government, but speaking for myself personally, my disposition would be to aid Capt. Bernier if there were resources coming from outside which would enable the expedition to take place.

It is a pity the government cannot give us some clear idea of its intentions in respect to this expedition. It is a well known fact that Capt. Bernier's chance of receiving subscriptions from the public generally and from scientific societies depends a great deal upon the assurance which the government will give to assist the project. In fact, at the present moment I believe Capt. Bernier has succeeded in obtaining promises of subscriptions to the extent of $20,000, although he has only been put in default to do so, a short time ago. There is no doubt whatever that if the government will promise to help him, he will very soon get the amount mentioned by the Prime Minister. Under these circumstances it is a pity that he should be put off for another year, and that in the interval the construction of the ship in which he is going to undertake his perilous voyage cannot be proceeded with. In view of the sentiments expressed in this House on more than one occasion the government might give him that promise of assistance which would enable Capt. Bernier to go courageously to work in obtaining these subscriptions, which he would undoubtedly obtain if the government would promise aid.

I very much regret that the government has not taken action to assist Capt. Bernier. I feel satisfied that no $70,000 could be spent by this government that would advertise Canada more throughout the whole world, even though the expedition should fail in finding the pole. If the government could see their way clear to bring down a further estimate for $75,000 or $80,000, to be paid over only when Capt. Bernier has secured private subscriptions for the balance of the money required, I have no hesitation in saying that in a very short time the entire sum would be contributed. The government then need not pay anything unless their grant was supplemented by outside subscriptions. It would be a matter of pride to every man in Canada if a native Canadian of the character of Capt. Bernier should be the first to place the British flag on the North Pole.

Yesterday I placed a resolution on the Order paper, asking the attention of the acting Postmaster General to the increase of salaries which, he admitted, he intended giving the letter carriers. I was one of the deputation that waited on the hon. the Postmaster General a day or two before he left, and he assured the deputation that the gentlemen he was leaving in charge of his department would see that the matter was carried through. Several deputations have since waited on the acting minister, and I think it would be a gracious act on his part to carry out the promise made by the Postmaster General. The letter carriers are a very deserving class of men and certainly have presented a case that is well worthy of consideration.

My lion colleague, the Postmaster General, had taken the matter Into consideration before he left, and had practically devised a scheme by which these men would be given an increase. I had two or three deputations of the letter carriers wait on me. There was some difference of opinion as to the best plan to be adopted, and after full consideration I concluded it was best to allow it to stand over until next session. I think that the letter carriers themselves were pretty well satisfied also to have the question remain over. While I am not in a position to say what will be done, I can assure my hon friend that the Postmaster General and the government are favourable to an increase, and that a plan will be adopted which will, I trust, meet the views of the letter carriers and the House generally.

I understand, from what the acting Postmaster General has said, that a plan had been drafted and that that plan had been submitted to the carriers themselves, who waited on the acting minister, and that the reason it was not put into effect is because there was difference of opinion among the letter carriers as to the best method of carrying it into effect. I said that we had discussed the various methods with the deputation.	.

In connection with this item, I would ask the Prime Minister a question with reference to a report cabled from London, to the effect that the premier of Newfoundland has been on a visit to Ottawa, that he has made an arrangement with the Canadian government by which it was permitted him to enter into a treaty with the United States, without Canada interfering. In the correspondence which took place between the Imperial government and the Canadian government, it was stated that no colony would be allowed to enter into a commercial treaty with a foreign country



*which would he iu any way detrimental to and other colony, and that on the receipt of any complaint in that regard the Imperial government would immediately disallow such a treaty. According to the cabled report, the Canadian government have withdrawn objection to the arrangement between Mr Bond, premier of the Newfoundland government, and the authorities at Washington to negotiate a commercial treaty without the consent of the Canadian government. Is there any truth in that report ?

There is no truth whatever in the statement which has been telegraphed from London, to the effect that the Canadian government had withdrawn their objection to the treaty known as the Bond-Blaine treaty, which was negotiated some ten years ago. Since that treaty was negotiated in 1890, as everybody is aware, a joint commission has been appointed by the governments of Great Britain and Canada. and the United States, with a view to settling many difficulties, amongst others the fisheries 'question, a question which is common to both Newfoundland and Canada. On that commission Newfoundland is represented. The commission has not yet accomplished any treaty, but it has not come to an end. It is simply suspended, and I have some hope-indeed, I have strong Pope-that the negotiations may be resumed at any early day, probably during the course of the year. As Newfoundland is a party to the negotiations, as she is represented by a commissioner, as she has accepted the invitation which was tendered to her some four years ago to participate in the acts of the commission, it seems only fair that before any further action is taken toy any government. whether the government of Great Britain or the government of Newfoundland, the negotiations of this commission should come to an end. Should the negotiations fail, or should they not be resumed within a reasonable time, or should they be resumed and not accomplish any purpose so far as the interests of Newfoundland are concerned, then the matter may be again opened for further consideration. But at present the matter remains just as I have stated ; and the position taken by the Canadian government, apart from the merits of any question, is that as there is a commission in existence to which Newfoundland is a party, the question ought to be left in abeyance.
As this question is up, is not now the i>roper time to resume negotiations with Newfoundland, looking to its joining this confederation ?
I have not heard of any disposition in Newfoundland to that effect yet.
But the right hon. First Minister did hear something in that direction under the old government of Newfound-
land, and I do not think he was favourable to the idea then.
When was that ?
Under the government of Sir James Winter. That government was friendly to the idea of joining the Dominion of Canada. I presume the First Minister knows that very well.
I am not aware of that.

Nothing apparently has been done to bring about such a union. Now, a new government has come in which is not so friendly, I assume, to the idea of confederation, as the late government was. In fact, it went to the United States and negotiated a treaty-one which was considered so detrimental to the interests of Canada by the then government of Canada, that it entered a most vigorous protest against that treaty being confirmed, and I think very rightly-perhaps we all think very rightly ; because the government of Newfoundland and the government of Canada have a kind of joint interest in the British fisheries on the Atlantic coast, and if that bad treaty had gone into force, there might have been conflicts, or there would have been powers given to the United States to which Canada had not consented, and which she would have been debarred from objecting to. Now, if nothing comes of this commisison, which we are told will probably resume its sittings this year, and if it does not succeed in accomplishing anything, then Mr. Bond will renew his demands on the British government to have the old treaty confirmed, and we may expect that the United States will be more anxious to make a treaty with Newfoundland than one with Canada, because they can apparently secure from Newfoundland terms that will suit them better than any they can get from the Dominion of Canada. The remedy for that is for the government to open negotiations for the admission of Newfoundland into the confederation. There are many other reasons for that; but this appears to toe the strong immediate inducement. The fisheries are along the Atlantic coast, the coasts of Newfoundland and the Gulf of St. Lawrence, being the joint possession of the two countries, and if Newfoundland were added to the confederation, Canada would have the undisputed right of dealing with these fishery questions with the United States, or with any other foreign power. I therefore say, for myself, that I think the government should take active measures to see if Newfoundland cannot be brought into the confederation of the Dominion of Canada. There would be manifold advantages in other directions. A sentimental consideration is that the whole of this northern part of North American continent would then be under one government, and our trade with Newfoundland and Newfoundland's trade with the rest of Canada

would be stimulated. It would be good for ibe trade of both countries. It would also be good in forming a still more loyal sentiment. But the government apparently have not made any move in that direction, principally, I presume, because the French shore question has not been settled, and they are afraid to touch any question in which the French nation might be brought into any hind of conflict with the Dominion of Canada. But, I do not consider that a reason why all negotiations should cease. I think rather that Newfoundland's ease, being apparently strong in itself, would be made infinitely stronger by the fact that not only the small province of Newfoundland, but the whole Dominion of Canada, would be directly interested in a settlement. The question must be settled. It has been pending in such an unsatisfactory conditon during these years and creating so much friction that it will have to be settled by the great powers ; and, to my mind, a settlement could be reached more quickly if Newfoundland were a portion of the Dominion. That colony is taking a position which seems to be a very moderate one, and one that could be readily defended, backed up by the Dominion of Canada, but I presume we will go drifting along doing nothing, as the government has apparently been doing, since the delegates were here some years ago.
I am not prepared to say whether the terms proposed, when Mr. Bond was premier of Newfoundland, were such as Canada should have accepted; but in a matter of such great importance I think we made a mistake if we allowed small financial considerations to interfere and prevent Newfoundland entering our confederation. That was a matter in which great national consideration should have outweighed the question of pounds, shillings and jience.
But since then our government has had greater opportunities, because there has been an administration in Newfoundland friendly to confederation, which the Bond government was not. The government appear to me, in this as in many other matters, would be simply drifting along without any definite policy. If they have a definite policy, they have not stated it to the House and the country.

I thoroughly agree with one or two remarks the hon. gentleman has made. There are international questions concerned, the settlement of which should not be governed by a mere consideration of dollars and cents. There was one occasion when our great scheme of confederation could have been completed by bringing Newfoundland into the Dominion. That was when the hon. gentleman himself was a member of the late administration. But that time unfortunately was allowed to go by. The material question of dollars and cents was allowed by the administration, 182*
of which the hon. gentleman was a member, to control this international matter. The hon. gentleman himself is responsible.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I was not a member of the cabinet.

He may not have been a member of the cabinet, but he was a member of the administration and is thoroughly responsible for the failure which overcame the efforts of that administration. And the general opinion has grown stronger more and more since that failure was due to a picayune policy of pounds, shillings and pence.
The hon. gentleman says that this gov-eminent has never laid down a policy with regard to the admission of Newfoundland. He is wrong. Two years ago that policy was laid down in clear and concise terms. Two years ago this government declared from these benches their anxiety to do everything possible to bring Newfoundland into the confederacy on any reasonable terms. There was nothing more we could do. If this government made any attempt within the past three years to force confederation on Newfoundland, that would have been a dismal failure. We have held out the right hand of fellowship; the people of Newfoundland know our views; and there is no evidence whatever that Newfoundland is willing to receive overtures. We hope the time will come when they will be willing to respond to our advances, but at present it would be most inopportune for us to make any further move in the matter. The hon. gentleman himself said that the time was not opportune.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I did not say that the time was not opportune to-day. On the contrary I said that it was not so opportune when the Bond government was in power as it was two years ago, under the government of Sir James Winter.

Since the failure of the negotiations undertaken by the late Sir John Thompson, of whose administration the hon. gentleman was a member and supporter, there has not been an opportune time when we could have negotiated effectively with Newfoundland.
speakername: The MINISTER. OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: There has been.

No. We have announced ourselves time and again as willing to resume those negotiations, and the government of Newfoundland are well aware of that fact. The hon. gentleman referred to the French shore question, but that question has ceased to be a material factor. It is now rather a sentimental one. The interests of the French nation on the west coast of Newfoundland are now merely sentimental, and those who have read the

views of the French admiral know that to he the case. The British government are anxious to deal with that question when the proper time arrives. My right lion, friend the First Minister has explained the course which Newfoundland lias taken since the initiation of the Joint High Commission, on which Newfoundland has a representative concerning the negotiations of that commission, and there seems to be no reason for taking the step the hon. gentleman has mentioned. As regards the bank fisheries, they are not the territorial fisheries of Newfoundland, nor do they belong to the Dominion. They are international. The key to the bank fisheries is in the fact that Newfoundland possesses the fresh bait. That is where the key lies. The hon. gentleman knows well that Newfoundland has been for years back negotiating with Canada and endeavouring to bring about a general treaty with the United States and Great Britain, which will cover the fisheries of Newfoundland as well as those of Canada. Judging by the expressions of opinion of the leading statesmen of Newfoundland, you could not do more harm than by making any overture at present for the purpose of bringing Newfoundland into confederation. Speaking-only for myself and not for the government, I am perfectly satisfied that any oversteps to bring about that union must come from Newfoundland herself. And when we have announced our cordial desire to entertain overtures that may be made by them, we have taken every step, I think, which ought properly to be taken by the Dominion to bring about a uniou. And I am perfectly sure that if you try in any way to take stejjs which would be looked upon by the mass of the electors of Newfoundland as forcing their hand, you will do more harm than good to the great scheme. The hon. gentleman can rest assured that the government are alive to the importance of the question.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Before the resolution is carried, I would like to say that if we have entered into negotiations, formal or informal, on the subject of the union of Newfoundland with the Dominion in the last four years, I am not aware that parliament has be0" informed of them.
I did not intend to say that there were negotiations. The hon. gentleman said that the policy of the government had never been announced, and I said that a few years ago it had been announced.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What was it ?

A cordial desire to bring about negotiations, but a statement that, under the circumstances, it was better that overtures should come from Newfoundland, because when we announced our desire to open negotiations, we had done all we
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: thought we should do, and that any effort beyond that would rather defeat than further the object in view.

I would gather from what the Minister of Marine and Fisheries says that there has been nothing in the way of negotiations, formal or informal. beyond the statement on the floor of parliament that the government is ready to entertain any overtures of the kind. The hon. gentleman refers to the efforts of the late administration and condemns as a picayune policy their policy in so great a matter. When he spoke in such terms as he did of failures on the part of the late administration, I think he must have forgotten some of the failures of the present administration. I do not know any more dismal failure than that which the hon. gentleman and his colleagues have made in carrying out their promises with regard to better trade relations with the United States. If he can point out a more dismal failure, I should like to have him do it. Is it due to a picayune policy on the part of this government ? He said there should be no picayune policy of dollars and cents in these great international matters. Is that why lie, as one of the members of the commission, failed to bring about an understanding with the great republic to the south of us ? I suppose that these matters of dollars and cents have to be regarded when negotiations are going on either with a great republic like the United States or with a province like Newfoundland. I think, perhaps, the hon. gentleman was speaking without the book when he referred as he did to the efforts of the late administration.

Do I understand the premier to say clearly that any commercial treaty which possibly might lie made between Newfoundland and the United States discriminating against Canada, this government would protest against?

I did not refer to that question at all. For, as I said, at the present time there is no occasion whatever to go into the merits of this question. At the present time, both Canada and Newfoundland are engaged in negotiations with the United States, with a view to settling questions in which Canada is concerned alone, and questions in which Canada is concerned with Newfoundland, and, so long as these are not matured in some way, there is no occasion to go into the question my hon. friend has alluded to. But I may say that, so far as I am informed, even if Newfoundland intended to negotiate with the United States, they have no intention of discriminating against Canada.
