There is one formal step yet to be taken In regard to the tariff. In the budget speech it was announced that no changes were to be made except with respect to the admission of certain materials for use in the construction of beet-root sugar factories. I desire now to move :
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Acts respecting customs duties by adding the following to the free list:-
Machinery of all kinds and structural iron and steel when imported under regulations to be made by the Minister of Customs for use in the construction and equipment of factories for the manufacture of sugar from beet roots until April 1, 1902.

I think it is very doubtful if any company will be able to take advantage of that ; but if it is done, it seems to me that it will be the part of wisdom to extend it for a longer time. It is only for about a year, and it takes so much preparation to build a factory that it is questionable whether any company would be jirepared to bring in machinery within that time. There is one I believe in contemplation. Whether it will be ready in time or not is very doubtful.

In view of the announcements which have already been made, I would hardly care to make a change now ; but if a case arises as suggested by the hon. gentleman, we can consider it on its merits. If this applicatiou had been made somewhat earlier, perhaps we could have taken some steps concerning it ; but as this provision was announced some time ago, I think we should deal with it as it stands, reserving to ourselves to deal with it later on should circumstances require an extension.

I do not believe that a single company or individual in this country will thank the Minister of Finance for this supposed concession. There is no concession about it. The matter was placed be-for the Minister of Finance and his colleagues by a large deputation of those interested who were forming companies ; and there will be no advantage taken of this provision during the limited time that the machinery is to be free. It is only a small matter, at any rate, because a large portion of the machinery would be made in this country anyway, in the ordinary course of things, and there would be no duty on that. But that industry is not going to be established under the conditions that at present exist, for I understand that one of these refineries costs $500,000 or $000,000. So that the supposed concession made by the Finance Minister does not amount to a row of pins.
Last year I think the rule was that all would be free of duty which could not be made in Canada. The government say that they have made a change, which they announce with a certain flourish of trumpets, as if it were very valuable and important that not only those machines which are not produced in Canada should come in free of duty, but all the machinery required, whether it can be made in Canada or not. I do not think that is going to be of any benefit to the starting of the industry in this country. It will require greater stimulus to induce people to invest the capital required to start an industry, which, in this country, is almost entirely experimental from the beginning.

Two weeks ago the agent of the Canada Atlantic Railway came to Renfrew. We held a meeting under the auspices of the board of trade, presided over by the mayor, and the agent of the Canada Atlantic stated that if the town of Renfrew would undertake to induce the farmers to grow the beets, there was an individual prepared to put $500,000 into a beet-root sugar factory in the town of Renfrew.

The hon. member for West York rather underestimates the importance of the concession. The deputation which waited on the government. while they would have been much pleased to receive further concessions, attach considerable importance to this one. The concession made a year ago limited to machinery not made in Canada was too restrictive. It was alleged that there were advantages in having the machinery of a beet-root sugar factory purchased in the one establishment abroad. If you expect to have a well-equipped factory, you would have to place your order in the hands of one person and allow him to get the whole machinery from abroad, because the getting of one portion in one place and another in another led to difficulties. If it costs $600,-Mr. FIELDING.
000 to establish a beet-root sugar factory, $400,000 would probably represent the machinery and structural materials, which will be free by this resolution, and the duty on that would be a considerable sum. It would probably be not less than $100,000. While they would have been well pleased to have had further advantages, the gentlemen who propose establishing this industry attached considerable value to this concession, and I hope there will be, as my bon. friend from Renfrew suggests, a disposition on the part of capitalists to put money into the enterprise on the encouragement offered. True they may have been scared off lately. Something has happened since this resolution was brought in. My hon. friends opposite, by numerous speeches, have advocated the removal of the duty on sugar, and that would be cutting off the protection which beet-root sugar has in Canada. They may thus thoughtlessly have scared off intending investors. But nevertheless I trust that the enterprise will be established,, and that the degree of encouragement we are giving will be appreciated.

It was the government that scared them off by not giving them the aid, in the shape of a bounty, that they are entitled to. The government are willing to give bounties for the manufacture of lead, and iron and steel and other lines, but they are not willing to give the farmer any assistance at all. There is a proposal to establish a beet-root sugar factory at Wallaceburg. But how ? By asking that small town to give a bonus of $50,000. Representations were made that in view of the fact that the government had given little or no assistance, they could not afford to establish a factory unless the locality gave them substantial aid. But it is unreasonable to force the people of a locality to tax themselves so heavily, when the object could be accomplished by the government giving a slight bounty on the sugar.
No matter what the government may do. the parties will always go to the municipalities for a bounty, and nothing we could do would prevent applications of that character.

1 am surprised to-learn the reason why the government increased the duty on imported sugar. It seems now that it was entirely for the purpose of encouraging the growth of the beet root and the manufacture of beet-root sugar. That certainly is a surprise to me, as no doubt it will be to other members. Last session the Minister of Finance made a very strong statement of the reasons why he increased the duty on certain atticles, and I presume that sugar was amongst these. He said that the government wanted to maintain a firm financial position. They wanted to have plenty of money to spend. * and because the duties had been reduced on

certain articles by* the preferential tariff, It was necessary to increase them on other articles, so as to make up the deficiency. When he reduced the duty on woollen goods In order to aid the workingmen of England, he felt bound to tax the workingmen of Canada so as to make up the deficiency. But now he says his object was to encourage the production of beet-root sugar. Yet he refuses to our farmers the assistance which he is willing to grant the smelters of lead in British Columbia, and the producers of iron all over the country. He refuses to grant any bounty, and it seems to me that his reasons must be a surprise to the whole House.

The argument of the Minister of Finance will hardly bear investigation. The hon. gentleman says that there will be $400,000 worth of importations for the proposed new factory, on which there will be a saving of $100,000 in duty. I stated that a large portion of the machinery could be got in Canada, but the minister replied that by buying the whole machinery from one firm you could secure a better outfit than by purchasing from different firms. I presume that the manufacturers of sugar refineries are not manufacturers of steam engines and boilers, and you would have to get those steam engines and boilers elsewhere. It will be immaterial, if you want a 400 or 500 horse power engine and boiler, whether you get it from one establishment or another, because they are all now made on certain plans, and our Canadian factories can turn out as good machines as you can get anywhere. But the building and the whole outfit must necessarily be made in Canada, even if some portion of the machinery come from the United States. I have no specific knowledge what these machines are, but I should suppose them to be rather in the shape of large tanks and boilers than in that of any intricate or complicated machinery. So, the saving by duties, I think, would be of the slightest character, and would not reach one-quarter as much as is estimated by the minister. Of course, that is a matter of opinion. The hon. gentleman has no data for his opinion, and I have not very much more. But the other point raised by the hon. gentleman for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), is very important. About $10,000,000 is spent by the people of Canada in importing the raw sugar or refined sugar, and syrup and molasses. It is proposed, if encouragement is given that all this shall be produced in Canada. It has been demonstrated, apparently. that we can grow the raw material, the sugar beet as well as any other place in the world. The standard requires 11 to 12 per cent of sugar in the beet for profitable production. But in Canada the percentage runs as high as even 17 or 18 per cent. The manufacture of sugar here
would mean the saving to the people of Canada of that $9,000,000 or $10,000,000in this way, that instead of sending the money out of the country, it should go to give employment to the people here, and we have plenty of people engaged in farming pursuits to do the work. So, an industry of that kind, I think, is one that ought to receive the first consideration of the government. But, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for East Grey, the government is preparing to give a most liberal bonus for the manufacture of iron and steel-amounting in this province, including what is paid by the Ontario government to $7 a ton, and $G per ton in the other portions of the Dominion-this bonus representing a large proportion of the cost of producing articles, as we learn from the prospectus of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. Then there is a bounty, a smaller bounty it is true, for the lead industry, and it is one that, so far as I am concerned, I approve of. But why should the farmers of this country, who are asking to have an opportunity of producing many millions of dollars' worth of beets, as well as the artisans and labourers who will be employed in the manufacture of sugar, be deprived of the opportunity by reason of this parliament adopting a different course from that which they adopted in the case of the iron and lead industry. It is utterly unjustifiable in my opinion. The principle having been adopted, and adopted on the most liberal scale so far as the manufacture of iron is concerned, the government should carry out that policy to its legitimate conclusion. And. where a case has been made out as it has in the case of the beet-root sugar industry in Canada, the Canadian farmers should he given an opportunity. The farmers are looking for that opportunity. All over the country the farmers find that they must look for new sources of revenue, and the production of the beet root is attracting their attention. And, while an opportunity for the develop-uient of a new industry is opening up to the farmers, it is set aside by the course taken by the government. And they are told that, instead of employing the Canadian manufacturer to produce their machinery, they are to be given an opportunity. and even encouraged, to go outside. For the minister has made the statement that his information is that it is better to buy the whole outfit from one house. What the reason for that is I do not know. I repeat that the farmers will not be satisfied with the course of the government, in its failure to adopt the same policy for the protection of the farmers in this industry as is given to the producers of the iron industry.

The argument of the hon. gentleman is that the encouragement here proposed will not be

effectual. Tlie lion, gentleman says that nothing will be accomplished by it. He says that the agricultural interests have been unjustly dealt with, because we have given a bonus for the production of iron and lead, and have not given a bonus in this case. But the hon. gentleman will see that there is a difference in the two cases. An iron mine is of no value to the owner or to the country unless the ore is wrought into iron-it cannot be turned to any other purpose. And the same way with the lead mine-its output can be nothing but lead. But the farmer with 100 acres of land is not in the position of being obliged to grow beets or grow nothing. The Ontario government have seen fit to bonus this production, and the Dominion government is going to the extent that is here proposed to encourage it. But for the hon. gentleman to say that nothing will be accomplished, is for him to take a position for which he is nol able to show any warrant. Hon. gentlemen opposite would not want this government to give more than is necessary to bring this industry into existence. The hon. member for Bast Grey (Mr. Sproule) tells us that the probability is that a factory will be established at Wallaco-burg. The Sugar Beet refining Company of this city have already made contracts in various sections surrounding London and St. Thomas for the growing of 400 acres of sugar beets. The company agrees to pay $3 a ton on board cars. They supply seed free.

organized for the purposb of beginning an establishment there. When the hon. gentleman says it guarantees them $3 a ton, I suppose the contracts will guarantee that amount at any rate. I am quite sure that does not mean that the London company proposed building a factory and manufacturing those beets in Canada, because a large number of contracts have been made at Wallaceburg for the Marine City Factory at $3.25 ai ton for beets laid down on the bank of the river. I do not see anything in the argument of the Minister of Customs that the protection of iron and the protection of the 100-acre farm are to be judged by two different standards. He says that if the iron is not converted into pig iron it remains there, and the man on the 100-acre farm can grow something else. That is just the difficulty. The farmer in western Ontario, we will say, where all these refineries are, finds that he has to give up growing wheat, that is practically what it means. He cannot make it a profitable industry at 65 to 70 cents a bushel, and even lower than that in many cases. In years gone by wheat and barley were the two great products of the farmers of western Ontario, as the Minister of Customs knows. They were looking round to find some other industry in which they could profitably be engaged, and grow other crops on their 100-acre farm ; and they made up their mind from what they had seen and heard, that sugar beets could#be produced here, and the refineries could be seen and heard, that sugar beets could because the farmer on the 100-acre farm has to turn his attention to some other industry that he is now very much disappointed.

To acquire from the Dames Ursulines de Quebec the property known as the Plains of Abraham, a sum not exceeding $80,000.

There has been a good deal of comment upon this matter in the newspapers during the last few weeks, and for some time since this matter has been discussed In Quebec, first by the Historical Society, then it went into the field of municipal politics, and then into the field of federal politics. A good many comments were made upon the position of the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dobell) in that matter. I regret to see that that hon. gentleman is not here in order to explain what were those great objections which he had, not only as the representative of the county where this property is situated, but as a member of the government also.
I beg your pardon. The property is in my constituency, and I have no objection to it.

The property is very close to the residence of the hon. member for Quebec West, and very close, I understand, to the property that was sold by his brother-in-law. Of course, all these matters have become of jmblic interest, and I think it would be well that the government should give the committee some explanation concerning the question. I would also like to know what were the reasons given to the government for the purchase of this property.

The property, which is known as the Plains of Abraham, is now owned by a religious community known as the Dames Ursulines de Quebec. It has been in their possession, I suppose, for some 200 years. It is now under a lease to the government of Canada, passed in 1803, for a term of ninety-nine years, which term expires on the 1st of May, 1902. After that date the possession of this property reverts to the Dames Ursulines. It seems to be the general impression, from certain rumours current, and probably true, that it is the intention of the Dames Ursulines, as soon as the property reverts to their possession, to divide it up into city lots and to sell them.
It has been represented to the government by numerous bodies, and numerous individuals, that it would be very proper indeed that this land, which is held by Canadians of all origins as sacred, should not be
allowed to pass into the hands of private parties, but that it should be acquired by the Canadian government and remain as a national property. The government share that view. The government is of the opinion that it would be most unfortunate if a ' property of that nature, about which so many historical associations are centered, were to be treated as ordinary property, bought, sold, divided into lots and treated as any other piece of land would be. Acting upon this consideration, we think that we meet the views of the House, that we meet the views of the Canadian people, when we ask parliament to authorize the purchase of this property. That is the reason, I may say in answer to the last question of the hon. gentleman, that has prompted us to ask for the appropriation that we are asking parliament to vote. There have been certain rumours to which my hon. friend has made allusion, as to which I wish to say a word. There have been certain allusions to the fact that the adjoining property of March- . moiit has been acquired by a certain gentleman with the view of exchanging it with the nuns who are the owners of the plains.
I am not concerned with these transactions. Whatever may have taken place in respect to this does not and cannot affect the government, because we ignore altogether any such transactions. We have no intention of buying any other property than the Plains of Abraham and no intention of dealing with any other parties than the owners of the property; that is the nuns. After we have bought the property and paid the money, whatever they do with their money, whether they buy real estate, or whether they put it in the bank, or use it in any way they see fit, it is no concern of ours. The only thing with which the House is concerned is whether or not we are paying a fair price. It is understood we can buy the property for $80,000, and I must say that at first blush when I heard that this property could be had for the price of $80,000, I thought the price was perhaps a little of an overcharge.
How many acres are there ?
There are seventy-one acres and a fraction.
Are those French acres or English acres ?
I think they are French acres.

No. English acres. I have a report from Mr. Genest, surveyor of the city of Quebec, who states that the property is 71 acres, English measure, equal to 84 and a fraction arpents, French measure. It was understood that the nuns estimated the value of the property at 10 cents a foot. When I received

this report I caused an inquiry to he made by two competent engineers and architects from the city of Quebec, Mr. Berlinguet and Mr. Peachy. They valued the property at 5 cents a foot, which would make it worth $130,000. Some time ago a deputation waited upon the government as to this question, and amongst the gentlemen who waited upon the government were some of the leading business men of Quebec. One was Mr. H. M. Price, who is well known as one of the leading merchants in Quebec. Another wras Mr. Victor Chateauvert, also a leading merchant and very well known in political circles, who was at one time the member for the central division of Quebec in the local legislature and who was the Conservative candidate for the local legislature in the last general election. These are gentlemen whose testimony is unimpeachable and whose respectability is above cavil. They both stated that in their opinion the property at $80,000 was cheap. They gave an opinion in writing, but another gentleman, the secretary of the delegation on that occasion, Mr. Chambers, told us in the presence of the delegation that he was authorized to say on behalf of Mr. Andrew Thomson, president of the Union Bank, and of Mr. Garneau, a member of the legislative council and other well known business men that the property was cheap at $80,000. I am glad to say that the opinion which I at one time held, that the price at $80,000 was perhaps too high has not been verified. Hon. gentlemen who are familiar with the city of Quebec are aware that for a great many years that city was, if 1 may say so. under a commercial cloud when -property, which at one time had been of great value, was very much reduced, and I am glad to say that at the present time there is a different condition of things prevailing in Quebec, that business is extending, that property is reviving and that property which could have been bought a few years ago for a nominal sum could not be bought now except at a very substantial price.
Is that property in the neighbourhood of the Plains of Abraham ?
All over the city.

There are some parts of the city, for instance, about the Cove at which we were looking which do not appear as if they were sharing in the prosperity that has undoubtedly manifested itself in some other parts of the city.

That will come. This Cove which the hon. gentleman saw the other day when he paid a visit to it, for which I am very thankful and very glad, was at one time the most valuable property in the city of Quebec. It has gone down, but there is no doubt whatever that when the bridge is built and when lue railway has been brought towards the Cove this Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
property will revive again, but in the meantime property in the upper parts of the city has increased very considerably. One of the leading merchants of Quebec is Mr. Gaspard Lemoine, and I must say he is not one of my political friends. He belongs to the Conservative party. I hold in my hand a letter in which he says that property on the other side of the street from where the Plains of Abraham are situated is worth from 20 to 35 cents a foot. He says :	If you
were to divide the property into two, if you were to put a street across the Plains of Abraham the property adjacent to what is known as Les Grande Allee would be worth $70,000, and the rest of the property between that street and the river would be worth at least $290,000. His estimate of the property is that it would be worth in the neighbourhood of $300,000-between $250,000 and $300,000.
Does the property go down to Champlain street ?

No, it goes down to the cliff. I do not pretend that the property can be sold to-day for the price that Mr. Lemoine names, nor do I believe it is his intention to convey that impression, but he says that if we were to divide the property into city lots to be sold as city lots it would be worth between $250,000 and $300,000. Under such circumstances I think that if we can secure the property for $80,000, we are getting it at a cheap price.

I saw it stated that the Ursulines had sold under certain conditions. I understood from the Prime Minister that the government was not concerned about any conditions, and that they had made the purchase of the property outright.

That is not what I said. I said that for our part we wanted to deal with the Ursulines alone, and we understand that the Ursulines are prepared to accept such an offer if we make it before the 1st of June, or thereabouts.
Is there a condition imposed by the Ursulines as to keeping the property up as a public park ?

We have had no negotiations with the Ursulines whatever. There have been voluntary negotiations between the mayor of Quebec and the Ursulines, but in view of this very rumour to which my hon. friend has alluded, we have carefully abstained from having anything to do with them, and we have declared ail along that we would not deal with them except with the Ursulines direct. We have had no negotiations with them up to the present time.

It seems to be the sentiment of the House that it is a wise thing for the government to purchase this property.

Speaking for myself, it seems to me that we have been too neglectful In the past of those historic spots. There are many In the province of Quebec which have now dwindled into instgnificance on account of our neglect. Certainly, a battlefield as interesting as this one, and fraught with such imperishable memories should be preserved to the nation if possible. For my own part,
I do not think that the price which is mentioned in the resolution is an excessive price for such an extensive property, situated in proximity to Quebec. I have no doubt that if it were divided into lots and utilized for commercial purposes, it might produce a much higher price than that mentioned in this resolution. But it seems to me that the right hon. gentleman has not answered satisfactorily the question of the member for Labelle. Whilst we all agree on the propriety of this transaction, there is no doubt that rumours have gone abroad that there was a deal contemplated-I think that is the proper expression-and that this purchase would not go through unless the Ursu-lines bound themselves to acquire another property which the vendors intended to part with, at a profit of $30,000. Those rumours were very widespread, and some colour of truth was given to them by the attitude taken by a member of the government. In view of these circumstances, I think that the right hon. gentleman should say that the government had made an investigation, and that it had come to the conclusion that no such deal was contemplated. Some assurance front the Prime Minister on that point, would have been very satisfactory to the House.

I think I can say that if my colleague from Quebec West (Hon. Mr. Dobell) were here, he would give my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) all the satisfaction he wants on that point. Mr. Dobell is not here to-day, but he will be here next session, and all the information can be given then. For my part. I am quite certain that nothing of the kind has taken place. But I must say to my hon. friend that even if anything had taken place, even if there had been such a deal, the government could be in no way responsible. We will deal with the nuns directly and with the Archbishop of Quebec, who is their legal adviser in these matters.
I think there has been a misconception in regard to this property. Have not these people been the owners for many years.

About 200 years, and we have been in possession under the lease for 100 years. Suppose it had been contemplated that there would be a purchase of the Marchmont property, it has been stated that Mr. Tanguay bought Marchmont with the intention of making an exchange with the nuns-suppose that occurred
we disclaim all responsibilty for that. I assert this at once, and I give to my hon. friend the statement now as the basis of the appropriation for which we ask parliament ? that the government has nothing to do directly, or indirectly, with anything of the kind. We do not propose to purchase Marchmont nor to exchange it for the Plains of Abraham. We do not propose to have any transaction with anybody except the nuns. If we pay the money we can have the property for $S0,000, on the condition that it be made a public park. We will deal with the nuns directly, and we will pay them the money. What they do afterwards is no concern of ours. Whether they buy Marchmont at $20,000, or $40,009, or $100,000, is no concern of ours.
Not even if they are obliged to.
My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) says that the price is fair and right, and I understand he wants the property to be bought. From whom can we buy it ? What does he want us to do ?
I think it is a case where the government should investigate.
Investigate wbat ?
Investigate if there is any truth in the allegation that the nuns cannot sell this property unless they bind themselves to buy this Marchmont property.
I can tell the hon. gentleman that there is no truth whatever in the statement.
That is what I wanted to know.

I have been informed that the nuns wanted it to be a public park and not divided.

There will be no objection in Canada to the government purchasing the Plains of Abraham. It is a historical spot. It is where the two races that are prominent in Canada shed their

blood together. A beautiful park there, nicely planted with trees and flowers, would be an attractive spot for all Canadians to visit. I have it from the bon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dobell; that property which he sold in that locality a few mouths ago was sold for about onc-lil'th the money that is being asked for this property to-day. Another feature of this transaction is that if the property is purchased by the government, I understand that it will be held as a public park in the interest of the city of Quebec. It is true, it is a historical spot, and a great deal of sentiment that we all like is connected with it, and we would like to owii the property; but if the people of Quebec require a park, they should endeavour to purchase it for themselves without expecting the Dominion of Canada to purchase it for them, and keep it for that purpose. I think the citv of Quebec will be likely to get practically nearly all the use it will be to anybody. The sightseer may go there out of curiosity, and it would be a very pleasant place to visit; but it will always be principally for the use of the people of Quebec, and I think they should purchase it for themselves. I do not think that the argument of the First Minister that if this property were cut up into small lots, a great deal more could be realized .from it. is much of an argument; because it would be necessary to spend money in making streets, and so forth, and a large part of the property would probably remain unsold for a long time before any return could be got from it. So that though a larger price might be realized from it if cut up and sold in that way it is no evidence that the property is worth the same per acre when sold en block. But what principally influences me is the fact, as I am told, that a few months ago property was actually sold in the same locality at Mr. ROBINSON (West Elgin).
about one-fifth the price that is asked for this property.

I do not wish to oppose this item at all; but some hon. members arc, I think, labouring under a wrong impression about this property being a historical spot. According to some historians, it is not the place where the battle of the Plains of Abraham took place. I have just read in the last report of the Royal Society of Canada, a most valuable paper by Mr. Doughty, one of the officials of the provincial government at Quebec, in which it is demonstrated beyond the shadow of a doubt that the -battle did not take place on that spot, but much nearer the city of Quebec; and he arrives at this conclusion after having quoted all the officers who served in and who wrote on the subject. It is a historical error to say that the battle took place on that ground. However, I am not opposed to the item.

I have just one word to say in reply to my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule), who thinks that the price is exaggerated. To this there is a very obvious answer. The nuns are not particular to sell; they do not care to sell. They are satisfied to keep the property, and divide it into lots. My hon. friend says it takes a long time to dispose of it in that way. So it does.
Why do they make it a condition that if the government purchase the property they shall keep it as a park ?

Because they have patriotism enough to sacrifice some profit and take this xn-ice for it on that condition. With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux), if we are to go minutely into what are called errors in history, I am afraid we shall have many of our illusions taken from us. We had better perhaps keep our illusions. Tradition says that this was the battlefield. Perhaps the actual collision between the French and the English troops may have taken place further to the east; but my hon. friend forgets that there were two battles- one in 1759, and the other on the 2uth of April, 1760, and there is no doubt that pai-t of the battle was fought on that very ground.

I do not rise for the purpose of making any objection to the vote or finding fault with the price, but I rise for a little information. We in the city of Toronto are very desirous of having parks, and when we think of acquiring a park, we do not think of coming to the government and asking the government to buy it. and hand it over to us under any excuse: but the corporation buys it. There appears to be a different view applied to Quebec. I am not finding fault with it: but the government need not be surprised, after

buying little bits of property all over the country, If demands are made upon them from Toronto and Hamilton and other cities. We have historical sjiots ; but if we came and asked the government to buy a park within the vicinity of the borders of Toronto for $80,000, what kind of a reception would we meet with ?
We are told that property in Quebec is going up by leaps and bounds, and that it is so valuable it is almost dangerous to go near Quebec just now, and yet this Dominion is asked to supply that city with a park. In fairness to the rest of the Dominion, the city of Quebec should undertake itself to purchase this particular park, even though it be a historic park, and even though some gentlemen want to knock all the romance out of it. The government should arrange with the city of Quebec so that the city will agree to maintain the park in perfect order, for when we once get it on our hands it will be too late to make any such arrangement.

I was not aware that the city of Toronto has such sacred property within its limits as the Plains of Abraham. If it has any property of that character, and if the demand of the city of Toronto that we should take it over be backed by the whole people of Canada, as in this instance, my hon. friend will receive the same treatment. We have had piles of correspondence asking the government to purchase the property-correspondence from Toronto, Quebec, Montreal, and all parts of Canada, but we have had no demand to buy an inch of property In Toronto on historic ground.

We are a little modest in Toronto, and would not have the cheek to ask the House and the government to do anything of the kind for us. But there are historic spots right inside the city of Toronto. There is the property there which is now the property of the government, which is historic, and which the city would like very well to have, and if you will hand it over to the city, we would get considerably more than $80,000 for it.
The historic spots in Toronto are where political battles were fought by William Lyon Mackenzie.
I would ask the Solicitor General if Wolfe's monument is included in the purchase of the Plains of Abraham ?
That is already Federal government property. All the property from the eastern limit of the Plains to the Citadel walls, except the small strip fronting on Grande Allee, is government property.
How is it the jail is built on that property ?
That was built previous to confederation, and an order in council was passed in 1872 or 1S73, giving the jail, with the ground immediately about it, to the province.
It would be only fair to ask the provincial government to remove the jail from the Plains of Abraham.
It is a fine building.
Yes, but very objectionable. If we are to have a public park, on the field of battle where Wolfe fell, we would be yielding to national sentiment by having the jail removed.
Might remove it to Lindsay.

We have no cause for a jail in Lindsay. Let it be taken down to the lower town of Quebec or somewhere else. I have consulted many military men in Quebec with reference to this question. They all point out that the bargain is a very fair one, that the property would bring much more than $80,000, and that, as the property which the nuns are going to purchase, will face on the Plains of Abraham, they will in that way be recouped to some extent. Our good friend from Toronto (Mr. Brock) has referred to historic ground in that city. Let me tell him that General Pyke, one of ike most famous explorers and travellers this continent has produced, led an American force to Toronto and was shot within the precincts of that city. I for one would not object to voting for the purchase of the grounds in order to make a park for die city of Toronto. More than that, I would be willing to allow the American sympathizers of General Pyke to erect a monument to him in that city, and also to allow the American sympathizers of General Montgomery to erect a monument to him in the city of Quebec. It displays very narrow spirit on the part of Canadians to object to our doing this. In the recent South African war, a British general had a monument erected on the field of battle over the remains of an officer who commanded the Boer forces. I do not see anything humiliating or demeaning in allowing our American friends to erect these monuments. I would also encourage the government in setting apart these historic spots. I drew the attention of the government to the old historic Huguenot fort of La tour at the mouth of the River St. John. The early Huguenot settlers in the maritime provinces are a race of which this country may well be proud. I would willingly support a resolution to preserve that fort, and also the forts of Annapolis and Beau-sejour on the border between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.

I regret that X cannot support this motion. My opposition to it does not arise from any financial point of view. I think that the price paid for the property is not exaggerated. From what I have heard and know of the property, the price is moderate. But what I object to is the spirit which prompts its purchase. I have no objection to commemorating everything historic which is sacred to the memory of the Canadian people as a whole. For instance, the battlefield of Chateauguay, where the Canadians made themselves illustrious in defence of their country.	XVe hoar very often-and
every time I hear it I applaud-of the necessity of building up Canada as one nation and leaving aside all recollection of past differences. But we are now asked to commemorate an event which, X admit, we not only must accept, but the consequence of which I accept as having been

An lion. MEMBER. A blessing.

I would not say exactly a blessing, but of having turned to the advantage of the country, and which the descendants of the brave French soldiers who fought there have accepted loyally. But there is something more than that in this matter. The movement that was started in Quebec, and which led to the acquisition of tills property, was for the purpose of our commemorating the last defeat of French arms in America, and the decisive victory of English arms. I acknowledge that the descendants of the English race are entitled to be proud of that triumph, just as we can boast of several victories of our ancestors. But I say that all such recollections should be effaced as much as possible.
Hon. gentlemen who went to Quebec on the late excursion, whilst walking on the splendid Dufferin terrace may have seen a small monument erected on the western side of the terrace and dominating the River St. Lawrence. The foundation of that monument was laid by an English Governor nearly one hundred years ago, to the memory of the two great generals who fought in that battle, Wolfe and Montcalm. There is upon that monument a Latin inscription, the text of which I do not remember, but the meaning of which is : ' Their valour gave them a common death, history a common fame and posterity has erected this monument. That should be the spirit presiding over everything we do to commemorate noble deeds in this country. The movement which was at the bottom of this purchase was started by a small handful of gentlemen in Quebec, gentlemen for whom I have the greatest respect, and to whose action I would not object if they wished to commemorate that event for their own sake. But, when the movement is carried to the parliament of Canada with the idea of celebrating the last defeat of French arms in America and glorifying the Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
final victory of England, I do not think it fair to ask the Canadian people at large to pay for that glorification. As I said at the beginning, I have no objection to the acquisition of the historic sites where the two races fought for the common defence of the Canadian soil. What we should seek to keep is not the remembrance of English victories, or of French victories, but of Canadian victories in defence of Canada ; and, whenever the government asks for means to commemorate such events, I shall give my vote in favour. But, in the words of the Minister of Public Works on one occasion, I would say : Let bygones be bygones. There are many dark pages in our history that have been turned-let them remain turned. The history of the Canadian nation does not go far back, but her life has been long enough that both races may find many great events to commemorate without going back to a period of history which, while it was glorious to both races, has also bitter memories for both. Though 1 think the spirit of the government was a good one, I do not think the spirit which brought this movement forward and forced it upon the government was a proper one or one that should lie encouraged in this country where we all want to have good remembrances and not to keep alive the memory of the sad events in our history.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bourassa) will reflect a moment, I feel sure he will change the views he has just uttered. He finds no fault with the monument erected to the memory of Wolfe and Montcalm. There is no Canadian who visits Quebec and looks at that monument but feels proud of his nation that we have been able to forget our differences and divisions in this tribute to the memory of the great men who lost their lives on the Plains of Abraham. But if he finds no fault with the idea which suggested the erection of a common monument to the memory of Wolfe and Montcalm, I ask why he should object when we propose to consecrate the ground where Wolfe and Montcalm met their death. Is it not the same idea after all ? And if he can look with pride on that monument cannot he look with greater pride on the ground on which these great men met their death ? To me it seems a noble idea that in this ground where our common ancestors shed their blood we should bury the last of those differences to which my hon. friend has made allusion. That is the thought that inspired those who approached the government on this question. That is the thought that has inspired.the government also-that we, should have another memento, that we should consecrate the very ground upon which these great men lost their lives and that it should remain free from polu-tiou for all time.

There seems to be a very general feeling that the money should be

voted for the purchase of these grounds. But I think there should be a clear understanding as to who is to maintain the park. I recollect when hon. gentlemen who are now on the Treasury benches were on this side of the House, many of them found fault with the government of that day for keeping up Major's Hill Park here. There should be a clear understanding that, if the land is purchased toy the Dominion, the city of Quebec should keep up the park.
Hear, hear.
Perhaps the right hon. Prime Minister will tell us what the grounds have been used for since they were leased.
The ground was leased for military purposes, to keep it as a military ground. It was used as a race course for many years
And grazing ground.

It has been put to no very special use.
Mr. 'WILSON. Is it understood that the city of Quebec will keep up the park ?
I think it should toe understood that the city of Quebec shall maintain it.

I do not think the city of Quebec should toe allowed to take that ground. There should toe a parade ground there. It may be very valuable for military purposes in the future. Referring to the remarks of the hon. member for La-belle (Mr. Bourassa), I am surprised that a gentleman of his chivalric nature should not see that in this very movement there is something that will have a tendency to fuse the two races even closer together. I pretend to be as loyal a man as he, but I can stand on the field, for instance, of Caril-lon# or Ticonderoga where the British met severe defeat at the hands of the French, and yet feel as patriotic a Briton as though the British had won.
Would you advise that they be bought ?

Certainly, if that could be. But, unfortunately, it is in Yankee territory. I have little sympathy with a man who, in this enlightened age, is so narrow that he would object to the purchase of a property of this kind on the ground that it would breed a feeling of race antagonism.

I regret the absence of the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dobell), and I think it is a pity that there should be any misunderstanding as to his attitude on this question. It has been suggested both here and in the press that that hon. gentleman opposed the acquisition of the Plains of Abraham. Whatever else may be said of the hon. member for
Quebec West, one fault he cannot be accused of, and that is want of loyalty or devotion to the best interests of the city of Quebec. He is a foremost citizen of Quebec, and has been most generous in his attitude toward the city. As a matter of fact, he was one of the warmest advocates of the acquisition of the Plains of Abraham. But he thought that property could be acquired for a less sum, and he was anxious that we should acquire it for a less sum. But, after investigation, we concluded that that could not toe, and this sum is therefore asked for. But anybody who gets the impression that the hon. member was not enthusiastic in his advocacy of the acquisition of the Plains of Abraham will do him a great injustice ; and in his absence I wish to state that fact.

I am quite sure that there was no intention-at least, I know that it was not my intention-to leave on the minds of hon. members the impression that the hon. gentleman from Quebec West was opposed to the purchase of the property, but only opposed to the purchase at the price offered, because he thought it was too high. And I still entertain the opinion that the government were buncoed a little by the nuns proposing to divide this property and sell it in lots. It was a business transaction and they used that as an advertisement, I think, that the government might be advised to buy. The very fact that they stipulated in the sale that it should not be used for any other purpose than a park, leaves that impression upon my mind. If they so much desired it to be a park, why did they threaten to divide it up into lots unless it be to get a higher price for it ? I would like to say one word with regard to the observations of the hon. member for Labelle. It did seem to me when the proposal was made to purchase this property, that if there was one thing more than another that ought to cement the affections of the two races, it would be the fact that the country had got a property that was sacred to both alike. After hearing him, I am disposed, with the consent of the committee, to withdraw all that I have said against the purchase.

I desire to enter an objec-ton to the argument made by the hon. member for West York, concerning the value of property in the city of Quebec. The inference which he has drawn from the dilapidated state of the property in the neighbourhood of the coves, is not justified. The depreciation of the value of that property has arisen from causes over which no merchant in the city of Quebec has any control. The forests of the country have been lessened, and the method of exporting wood has been changed, as a result of which that property has become almost absolutely valueless for the purposes to which it was put thirty years ago. Those gentlemen who visited the city of Quebec a few days ago saw the

disadvantages under which the city had laboured on account of the decay of that [DOT] industry, and the same remark will apply to the decay of the industry of wooden shipbuilding. Notwithstanding these hinderances, those gentlemen saw the prosperity which is evident throughout the town itself, the fine streets, the new buildings, the factories that were seen not only In the upper town, but in St. Roch and St. Sauveur. They could see that this city had prospered mightily in spite of the drawbacks. Now, as regards the price of this property, I do not pretend to be an expert, but I know Mr. Price, and Mr. Chau-teauvert, and nearly all the other gentlemen whose names have been mentioned by the right hon. Prime Minister. They are men in whom I have eveiy confidence, and I am delighted to see that this property is being purchased.
